posts.title: Patent Prior Art, Indigenous Knowledge, and the Nagoya Gap
posts.summary: The psychedelic compounds now at the center of a rapidly expanding commercial industry Psilocybe mexicana in Veracruz, Mexico.

slides.alt: The glass-fronted atrium entrance of the Madison Building, headquarters of the United States Patent and Trademark Office in Alexandria, Virginia, seen across a lawn on a clear day. It is the agency where the patent prior art rules discussed in the article are applied.

Psilocybe mexicana, the mushroom from which Albert Hofmann first isolated psilocybin in 1958, in a field photograph from Veracruz, Mexico, July 2, 2019: a cluster of small tan conical caps on slender stems growing in grass.

Peyote, Lophophora williamsii, in a field photograph from south Texas, April 30, 2020: a blue-green spineless cactus with rounded ribs and tufts of wool, flowering with two pale pink blossoms at its crown, beside a second plant, on dry ground. It is one of the plants the article names.
The first page of Public Law 112-29, the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act, signed September 16, 2011, 125 Stat. 284, as published by the U.S. Government Publishing Office.

A crop of 35 U.S.C. 102 in the 2024 edition of the U.S. Code: the section heading, Conditions for patentability; novelty, and subsection (a)(1), which bars a patent when the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date.

A crop of the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure, section 2152.02(d), with the sentence: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1), there is no geographic limitation on where prior public use or public availability occurs.

A crop of 35 U.S.C. 122(e), Preissuance submissions by third parties, in the 2024 edition of the U.S. Code: any third party may submit a patent, published application or other printed publication for consideration in a pending application, in writing, within the time the statute sets.

The page of 21 C.F.R. 1307.31, Native American Church, in the April 1, 2024 edition of the Code of Federal Regulations, stating that the Schedule I listing of peyote does not apply to nondrug use in bona fide ceremonies of the Native American Church.

A crop of page L 150/65 of the Official Journal of the European Union, 20 May 2014: Regulation (EU) No 511/2014, with the definition of traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources and Article 4, Obligations of users, which requires users to exercise due diligence that genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge were accessed under applicable access and benefit-sharing rules, and to pass the documents on to later users.

A side wing of the Nagoya Congress Center in Nagoya, Japan, with a blue sail-shaped clock sculpture and a raised walkway under a clear sky, photographed in 2018. The tenth meeting of the parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity was held here from 18 to 29 October 2010 and adopted the Nagoya Protocol on 29 October 2010, the first date on the card.
A crop of Public Law 112-29, section 3, 125 Stat. 285 to 286, with the new text of 35 U.S.C. 102, including the phrase otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date.

The East Front of the United States Capitol seen from the northeast on a clear day, with the dome and the Senate wing steps. Congress would have to pass the first direction on the list, a domestic benefit-sharing statute.

onScreen: Where the America Invents Act’s prior art standard may reach traditional knowledge in the psychedelic industry
The psychedelic compounds now at the center of a rapidly expanding commercial industry Psilocybe mexicana in Veracruz, Mexico.
have been used for centuries by indigenous communities in the Americas, Africa, and elsewhere for healing, ceremony, spiritual practice, and the transmission of cultural knowledge across generations.

Among the possible legal intersections between traditional indigenous knowledge and commercial psychedelic development, the patent prior art doctrine may be the most concrete and the most readily litigable.
AIA prior art has no geographic limit Public use, sale or disclosure anywhere in the world may qualify if it made the claimed invention available before the effective filing date.
The AIA created a formal mechanism by which any member of the public may submit prior art to the USPTO for consideration in the examination of a pending patent application.
Federal Indian law protects peyote only One plant, one set of users, ceremonial purposes. The article reads this as the ceiling of federal protection for Indigenous psychedelic use.

The Nagoya Protocol: international norm without US obligation US non-ratification removes any direct legal duty. EU partners still owe due diligence under Regulation 511/2014 and may pass it on to US firms by contract.
What We Actually Know
Directions the article raises, not existing law

glossary.definition: Under the AIA, a disclosure has no geographic requirement to qualify as prior art: prior public use, sale, or other disclosure anywhere in the world may qualify if it makes the claimed invention available to the public before the effective filing date.

Some commercial psychedelic operators have developed voluntary benefit-sharing arrangements, formal or informal commitments specifying a percentage of revenues, credit to indigenous knowledge holders, or support for indigenous-led healing programs.

posts.title: Nevada put medical cannabis in its constitution
posts.summary: Nevada voters said yes to Question 9 in 1998 and again in 2000. Here is the section they added, the two-vote rule that made them vote twice, the official counts, and what the text left for lawmakers to build.

slides.alt: The Nevada State Capitol in Carson City, a stone building with a silver dome, seen at the end of a walk lined with trees, lamp posts with Battle Born 150 banners and flagpoles; no people in frame. Slide text: Nevada put medical cannabis in its constitution. The Nevada State Capitol, Carson City. Voters approved Question 9 in 1998 and again in 2000. It became Article 4, section 38.

A crop of the Nevada Legislature's page of the Nevada Constitution: Article 4, section 38, Use of plant of genus Cannabis for medical purposes, subsection 1 and paragraph (a) listing the conditions. Slide text: The text is an order to lawmakers. Section 38 begins: "The legislature shall provide by law for" use by a patient, on a physician's advice, for listed conditions.

A crop of the scanned 1998 Nevada ballot booklet: Question No. 9, Amendment to the Nevada Constitution, and the condensation asking whether to allow the possession and use of a plant of the genus Cannabis for certain illnesses. Slide text: 1998: the question on the ballot. Question 9 asked whether to allow possession and use of cannabis for certain illnesses, on a physician's advice, with parental consent for minors.

A crop of the Nevada Secretary of State's 1998 Official General Election Returns: the Yes and No rows for Question 9 with one column per county, totals 241,510 yes and 170,264 no. Slide text: First vote: 58.7 percent yes. Official 1998 returns: 241,510 yes and 170,264 no. Ten of Nevada's 17 counties voted yes.
slides.credit: Source: NV Sec. of State, 1998 returns

slides.alt: A crop of the Nevada Constitution, Article 19, section 2(4): if a majority approves, the Secretary of State shall publish and resubmit the question at the next succeeding general election, and a second approval makes it part of the Constitution. Slide text: One yes was not enough. For an initiative amendment, Article 19 sends the question back to voters at the next general election. It needs a second majority.

A crop of the Secretary of State's letter in the 2000 Nevada ballot booklet: Ballot Question Number 9 passed at the 1998 General Election and appears for the second and last time on the 2000 General Election Ballot. Slide text: 2000: "the second and last time." The Secretary of State's 2000 ballot booklet said Question 9 passed in 1998 and was back for its final vote.

A crop of the scanned 2000 Nevada ballot booklet: Question No. 9 and its condensation, with 381,947 written by hand beside Yes, checked, and 202,211 beside No. Slide text: Second vote: 65.4 percent yes. Official 2000 results: 381,947 yes and 202,211 no. Only Lincoln and White Pine counties voted no.

A crop of the Nevada Constitution, Article 4, section 38(1)(d) and (e): a registry of patients and their attendants that law enforcement may use to verify a claim and that is otherwise confidential, and authorization of appropriate methods for supply of the plant. Slide text: A registry, and a way to supply. The Legislature must create a confidential registry police can check, and authorize "appropriate methods for supply." The text does not say which.

A crop of the Nevada Constitution, Article 4, section 38(2): the section does not authorize use other than medical or medical use in public, or require reimbursement by an insurer or accommodation at work, with the note that it was approved in 1998 and 2000. Slide text: What section 38 does not do. No non-medical use, no medical use in public, no required insurance payment. Insurance and patient access are on the MJBizCon 2026 program, Thursday, Dec. 3.

A crop of page 3053 of the Statutes of Nevada 2001: Assembly Bill No. 453, Assemblywoman Giunchigliani, Chapter 592, an act exempting the medical use of marijuana from state prosecution in certain circumstances, approved June 14, 2001. Slide text: 2001: the Legislature answered. AB 453 became Chapter 592, approved June 14, 2001; most of it took effect Oct. 1. A companion piece covers 2001 to 2015.

posts.title: Three stripes, four emails
posts.summary: In 2023 a Manhattan jury decided that Thom Browne's four bars did not infringe adidas's three stripes. Months later, four internal emails surfaced in a London lawsuit, and they said the bars could "look like Adidas." The court papers show what happened next, and why the emails never got the case reopened.

slides.alt: A typed court form headed Verdict, with handwritten check marks beside Not Liable for trademark infringement and for trademark dilution, and blank damages lines.
Printed court text quoting an email: as Adidas has such a big presence in the sporting world, it is inevitable that our 4bar in white be read as adidas stripes, especially on accessories.
Printed court text saying a paralegal had carried out a mass edit on documents that hit on the search term adidas, including the four emails, changing their fields to needs further review.
Typewritten court text ending: An inadvertent but understandable mix-up is not the same as negligence, at least not here.

Printed court text: because misconduct under Rule 60(b)(3) does not encompass merely negligent discovery violations, and Thom Browne's failure was no more than negligent, adidas is not entitled to relief.
Printed court text saying likelihood of confusion is an objective standard and the emails reflected executives' opinions, then that adidas's consumer survey did not persuade the jury.
The west front of the U.S. Supreme Court building at dusk, its white columns lit from inside above wide steps.

onScreen: Three stripes, four emails. In January 2023 a jury found Thom Browne not liable for infringing adidas's three stripes. The emails came later.
Four internal emails surfaced in a London case. One said it was "inevitable that our 4bar in white be read as adidas stripes." The New York jury never saw them.
A mass edit kept them out of the case. A paralegal tagged documents that hit on "adidas" as "needs further review," so the privilege search skipped them.
2024: the trial judge called it a mix-up. Judge Rakoff held that negligence could count as misconduct, then found the law firm had not been negligent.
2026: negligent, but not misconduct. The Second Circuit found the firm negligent and held that negligence alone cannot reopen a final judgment.
Confusion is an objective test. The emails were executives' opinions, the court wrote, and adidas's own consumer survey had not persuaded the jury.
Now adidas has asked the Supreme Court. It asks whether a negligent failure to produce documents can be misconduct. Thom Browne's reply was due Dec. 2, 2026.

glossary.definition: adidas is known for what the courts call its Three-Stripe Mark: three parallel lines of roughly the same width, placed close together.
Judge Rakoff had told the jurors to weigh a list of factors that courts in the circuit use to judge whether confusion is likely, known as the Polaroid factors after a 1961 case
Gross negligence usually means skipping widely recognized steps, such as never issuing a written instruction to preserve documents

posts.title: Protection without a storefront: Nevada medical cannabis, 2001 to 2016
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. Nevada's constitution asked for a way to supply patients. The first law gave them a card and a plant limit, and left supply to the patients. This part follows the documents from that law to a 2013 Senate hearing.

slides.alt: An aerial photo of the Nevada State Capitol in Carson City: a sandstone building with a white cupola and flags, bare spring trees and hills behind; no people in frame. Slide text: The constitution promised a supply. The first dispensary came 15 years later. Nevada's Capitol in Carson City, 2025. Voters put medical cannabis in the constitution in 2000. The state dates its first dispensary to August 2015.

A crop of a Nevada Legislature exhibit reprinting the state constitution, Article 4, section 38, paragraphs (d) and (e): a confidential registry of patients and attendants, and authorization of appropriate methods for supply of the plant to patients. Slide text: The constitution asked lawmakers for a supply. Article 4, section 38 called for a confidential patient registry and "appropriate methods for supply of the plant" to patients.

A crop of Nevada Assembly Bill 453 of 2001, in blue italic type: do not, at any one time, collectively possess, deliver or produce more than one ounce of usable marijuana, three mature marijuana plants and four immature marijuana plants. Slide text: 2001: the seven-plant cap. AB 453 let a cardholder and caregiver hold, together, one ounce of usable marijuana, three mature plants and four immature plants at any one time.

A crop of Nevada Assembly Bill 453 of 2001, paragraph (f): delivering marijuana for consideration to any person, regardless of whether the recipient lawfully holds a registry identification card. Slide text: Selling it stayed a crime. The same law gave no exemption for delivering marijuana "for consideration" to any person, even another cardholder. Patients could grow it or receive it free.

A crop of Nevada Assembly Bill 453 of 2001, section 30.5: the department shall vigorously pursue federal approval to establish a bank or repository of seeds, and a program to produce and deliver marijuana to people using it under the law. Slide text: The state supply plan stalled. AB 453 told the Agriculture Department to seek federal approval for a seed bank and a state supply program. A 2012 court order said: "This has not been done."

A crop of a scanned, line-numbered Nevada district court order, lines 21 to 26: the law strips anyone possessing marijuana in a place open to the public of the exemption, which necessarily prevents any store front medical marijuana provider. Slide text: A judge said no store could open. In February 2012, Judge Donald Mosley wrote that the law "necessarily prevents any store front medical marijuana provider." The state appealed. A 2014 report says the top court reversed.

A crop of Nevada Senate Judiciary Committee minutes: William J. Baker says he is a retired autoworker and disabled American, that without dispensaries he let his license expire, and that he was unable to grow his own and there was no place to buy it. Slide text: "There was no place to buy it." A retired autoworker told senators in March 2013 he let his card lapse. He was disabled, could not grow his own, and Nevada had no dispensaries.

A crop of Nevada Senate Bill 374 of 2013, section 11: dispensary certificates of 40 in a county of 700,000 or more, 10 in a county of 100,000 to 700,000, 2 in a county of 55,000 to 100,000, and 1 in each other county. Slide text: 2013: dispensaries capped by county size. SB 374 set 40 dispensary certificates for the largest county, 10 for the next size, 2 for mid-size counties and 1 for each other county.

A crop of the Nevada medical marijuana program web page timeline: 519 applications in August 2014; 372 provisional certificates on November 3, 2014, 55 of them for dispensaries; first final certifications in March 2015; first dispensary opening in August 2015, in Sparks. Slide text: 2014: 372 provisional certificates. They came from 519 applications filed Aug. 5 to 18. The Division dates the first dispensary opening to August 2015, in Sparks. It names no store.
slides.credit: Source: Nevada DPBH web page, 2017 copy

slides.alt: A Nevada health division presentation slide headed Who is fully operational, as of March 16, 2016: dispensaries 33 percent, 22 of 66; cultivation 38 of 182; production 17 of 118; laboratories 7 of 17; aggregate 84 of 383. Slide text: By March 2016, 22 dispensaries were fully operational. The Division's count for March 16, 2016: 22 of 66 dispensaries "fully operational." That was about 15 years after voters approved the amendment.

posts.title: Hawaiʻi Once Powered a Barge with the Temperature Difference in the Ocean
posts.summary: In 1979 a small barge off Keāhole Point turned the gap between warm surface water and cold deep water into net electricity. The hearings, reports and pipes it left behind show what it proved, and what it never set out to prove.

slides.alt: A halftone photograph of the Mini-OTEC barge afloat off Keāhole Point, Hawaiʻi Island, 1979.
slides.url: https://www.osti.gov/biblio/5390257 (report p.3, Figure 4; PDF https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/5390257, PDF page 8)

slides.alt: a tall rectangular plate-and-fin heat exchanger standing in an industrial hall (credited to Argonne National Laboratory), with a flanged pipe at the top and an inset showing its finned cross-section. It is an OTEC test unit of the kind in which warm seawater boils a working fluid; it is not Mini-OTEC hardware.
slides.credit: Photo: Argonne Lab, via DOE/SERI, PD
slides.url: https://www.osti.gov/biblio/5390257 (report p.9, Figure 1.7, PDF page 14; credited Courtesy of ANL)

slides.alt: An aerial photograph of the land-based experimental open-cycle OTEC plant at Keāhole Point, Hawaiʻi Island, which ran from 1993 to 1998: a tall round concrete vacuum vessel at lower left with white seawater pipes running past it, low buildings, a parking area and the lava coast with the Keāhole lighthouse at upper right. It is the other approach Hawaiʻi tested, not the Mini-OTEC barge. Low resolution (797 px), the best copy found.
slides.credit: Photo: US DOE (Luis Vega, AIP), PD
slides.url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OTEC_in_Hawaii.jpg (Commons gives the source as the Hawaii DBEDT page hawaii.gov/dbedt/ert/otec_hi.html and tags it PD-USGov-DOE); the same aerial photo is credited to Luis Vega at https://www.eurekalert.org/multimedia/888521

slides.alt: Lockheed's 1979 location map of the Hawaiian Islands with an inset of Keāhole Point: the Mini-OTEC mooring site is marked about 1 mile offshore. Card: first net power August 2, 1979; a little over a mile offshore; water about 80 degrees Fahrenheit at the surface and about 43 from the deep; about 50 kilowatts gross.

Lockheed's 1979 slide titled Results to Date, listing net power 15 months after go-ahead and 10 kilowatts electric of net power, as calculated. Card: about 40 kilowatts for pumps and other equipment; net output 10 kilowatts per Lockheed, 10 to 12 per the OTA, about 15 in a 1980 trade report.

Lockheed's 1979 system diagram: the Mini-OTEC barge, a support buoy, a 24-inch outside-diameter cold water pipe hanging 2170 feet, a crossover hose and a mooring line to a concrete anchor. Card: 24-inch polyethylene pipe about 2,150 feet long; run of about 2 months per the OTA, or about 600 hours through November 18 per a 1980 trade report.

A black-and-white halftone photograph from a 1980 Department of Energy brochure, captioned Mini-OTEC producing electricity off the coast of Hawaii: the barge seen from the stern quarter with MINI OTEC on the hull and plant equipment on deck. Grainy and under 1600 px, the best copy found.

slides.alt: a tall steel frame structure carrying large white pipes and a Makai Ocean Engineering sign, the company's OTEC research facility at Keāhole Point, photographed in 2019 under a blue sky. It is a later plant with its own pumps and pipes, not the 1979 barge, and stands for a plant whose auxiliary load comes off its gross output.

heavy surf and spray breaking over a lava shelf at the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii, with the lines of three seawater pipes running out through the surf zone, from a 1989 report. They are later pipes at the Keāhole site, not Mini-OTEC's pipe, and show how exposed such pipes are.
slides.credit: Photo: NELH, via DOE/SERI, Public domain
slides.url: https://www.osti.gov/biblio/5390257 (report p.14, Figure 2.2, PDF page 18; credited Courtesy of NELH)

slides.alt: the Makai Research Pier at Waimānalo, Oʻahu, a concrete pier on piles running over turquoise water to a tan hangar-like building with a green slope behind, photographed in 2008 by Ossewa. It is the ocean-engineering test pier of Makai Ocean Engineering, shown as a structure that has to live in salt water. It is not a seawater pipe, not Keāhole and not OTEC equipment.

A black-and-white photograph of workmen assembling the long black polyethylene cold-water pipe for Mini-OTEC at the water's edge, with a mobile crane lifting a section; the 1980 DOE brochure calls it the 2000-foot cold water pipe. Lockheed and the OTA give 2,150 feet.

posts.title: Nevada borrowed its cannabis regulator from the casino floor
posts.summary: In 2019 Nevada built its Cannabis Compliance Board from the parts of its gaming regulator. The statutes show what was copied, what was changed, and what the Legislature took back in 2023 and 2025.

slides.alt: The Nevada Legislative Building in Carson City on a sunny day: a pale stone building with a silver dome behind trees, a street lamp and a low wall reading Nevada State Assembly; no people in frame. Slide text: Nevada borrowed its cannabis regulator from the casino floor. The Legislative Building, Carson City. AB 533 was heard here in 2019. It made a cannabis board modeled after the Gaming Control Board.

A crop of page 2 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533 (2019): the digest sentence saying section 54 creates the Cannabis Compliance Board of five members appointed by the Governor and generally modeled after the Nevada Gaming Control Board. Slide text: The bill named its model. AB 533's digest calls the five-member Cannabis Compliance Board "generally modeled after the Nevada Gaming Control Board." It took over from Taxation on July 1, 2020.

A crop of typed minutes of the Nevada Assembly Committee on Judiciary, May 21, 2019, page 8: the Governor's general counsel says the structure is a lighter one of roughly 45 people as opposed to the 400 in gaming. Slide text: Similar to gaming, but lighter. The Governor's general counsel told lawmakers the cannabis board would have roughly 45 people "as opposed to the 400 in gaming." Those are his estimates.

A crop of page 4 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533: subsection 3 of section 3, saying public confidence and trust can only be maintained by strict regulation of all persons, locations, practices, associations and activities related to cannabis establishments. Slide text: A purpose clause from gaming. Like NRS 463.0129, section 3 says "Public confidence and trust can only be maintained by strict regulation of all persons, locations, practices, associations and activities."

A crop of page 14 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533: section 55, the board seats for investigation or law enforcement, a Nevada attorney, the cannabis industry, and a physician, psychologist, counselor or social worker. Slide text: Five seats instead of three. Like gaming's board, it has a finance seat and an investigator seat. It adds a lawyer, an industry seat and a health or counseling seat.

A crop of page 9 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533: section 52, creating the Cannabis Advisory Commission to study issues and make recommendations to the Cannabis Compliance Board. Slide text: One board, no second tier. In gaming, the Control Board investigates and the Gaming Commission decides. Cannabis has one board. Its Advisory Commission only recommends.

A crop of page 111 of Nevada Assembly Bill 533: the end of the list of agencies exempted from the Administrative Procedure Act, with the new entry (o) The Cannabis Compliance Board in blue type. Slide text: It took the rulebook exemption. AB 533 put the cannabis board on the list of agencies exempt from Nevada's Administrative Procedure Act. The Gaming Control Board and Commission were already on it.

A crop of page 3 of Nevada Senate Bill 328 (2023): new paragraph (f), with the word The struck through in red and blue text saying Nevada seeks to emulate other licensed, strictly regulated privileged industries insofar as their approaches are compatible with cannabis. Slide text: In 2023, a limit on copying. SB 328 says Nevada seeks to emulate other privileged industries "insofar as" those industries are similar or their approaches are compatible with cannabis.

A crop of page 17 of Nevada Senate Bill 328 (2023): the line (n) The Cannabis Compliance Board in brackets and struck through in red, below two other agencies on the exemption list. Slide text: The same law ended the rulebook exemption. SB 328 struck the Cannabis Compliance Board from the exempt list. The Gaming Control Board and the Gaming Commission are still on it today.

A crop of page 5 of Nevada Assembly Bill 76 (2025): section 5, saying the Board shall appoint one or more hearing officers to conduct hearings and render decisions. Slide text: Since 2025, hearing officers hear discipline cases. AB 76 moved disciplinary hearings from the board to hearing officers. The board reviews a decision only if a party asks or it acts on its own.

posts.title: Hawaii Home Grow Rules, Plainly
posts.summary: What Hawaiʻi's statutes, its health department's rules and its 2025 laws say about growing medical cannabis at home, laid out in the order a grower meets them.

slides.alt: First page of Act 46, Session Laws of Hawaii 2025 (S.B. 1429), stamped Approved by the Governor on May 14, 2025, titled Relating to Medical Cannabis, with the start of the Legislature's findings.

Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329-130 as the legislature's page prints it: a patient gets medical cannabis from a dispensary, by cultivating an adequate supply, or from a caregiver who cultivates one, with each growing location limited to five qualifying patients.
Page of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329-121 holding the definition of adequate supply, which caps the supply at ten cannabis plants, whether immature or mature.

Botanical plate of Cannabis sativa L. from Thomé's Flora von Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz, 1885: a male flowering stem, a female stem with seed heads and long toothed leaflets, and numbered details of flowers and seeds.

Page 6 of Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-160 (compiled February 15, 2019) with the definition of grow site: a specific location designated by the patient, which must be the patient's or caregiver's residential address or another location they own or control.

Page 24 of Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-160, compiled February 15, 2019, showing section 11-160-31: a patient or caregiver designated to cultivate shall have a legible identification tag on each cannabis plant being cultivated for the patient.

Left column of page 3 of OMCCR's Hawaiʻi Medical Cannabis Newsletter of May 2024, the grow site compliance guidance: one designated grow site, a ten-plant total at any stage, a tag on each plant, and handling only by the patient or the caregiver named on the card.

Page 6 of Act 46 showing amended section 329-130: a dispensary, patient cultivation and caregiver cultivation as lawful sources, each growing location limited to not more than five qualifying patients, and the old caregiver ban struck through.

Page 21 of Act 241, Session Laws of Hawaii 2025, showing part IV and the start of the new section on cannabis cultivator licenses, which begins Notwithstanding section 329D-24, it shall be unlawful for any person to cultivate cannabis without a license issued by the department.

onScreen: Hawaii home grow rules, plainly What the statutes, the rules and OMCCR's own pages say. Education, not legal advice.
Three lawful sources. Since Act 46, a patient gets cannabis from a licensed dispensary, by growing an adequate supply, or from a caregiver who grows it.
Ten plants at any stage. A patient's adequate supply is ten plants, immature or mature. OMCCR says a clone counts as one plant.
The plant the rules count. Cannabis sativa L., in a botanical plate from Thomé's Flora von Deutschland, 1885. The limit counts each plant, immature or mature.
The grow site goes on the card. It is the patient's residence, the caregiver's residence, or another site the patient or caregiver owns or controls.
Every plant wears a tag. The tag shows the 329 number and expiration date, hangs from or around the bottom, and must be readable from outside the plant.
Two people may touch them. Only the patient and the one caregiver on the card may handle the plants. A grow site or cooperative cannot be a caregiver.

onScreen: The ADA’s illegal drug use exclusion and state-licensed psilocybin services: where disclosure and protection may diverge

Psilocybin remains Schedule I When an employer acts on current use, the ADA’s illegal drug use exclusion under 42 U.S.C. § 12114(a) appears to apply regardless of state licensing or therapeutic intent.
The disclosure dilemma The disclosure that appears necessary to obtain accommodation may also tell an employer about use the ADA does not protect.
Psilocybin is not on the test panel A negative federal panel test is not legal clearance. The ADA lets employers prohibit illegal drug use at the workplace.
The testing gap is not a safe harbor A commercial driver who uses psilocybin would likely violate DOT rules on duty, whether or not a panel test detects it.
Off-duty protection may need a state statute Colorado’s Supreme Court held a state-licensed medical cannabis patient could lawfully be fired for failing a drug test.

posts.title: In Clark County, cannabis regulation can reach the magazine and the consultant
posts.summary: Clark County's licensing packet names cannabis magazines and consultants as support businesses. Here is what the county code, three county ordinances and Nevada's advertising law each say, where they differ, and what the documents do not show.

slides.alt: The sandstone pyramid of the Clark County Government Center in Las Vegas, 2011, seen up close with a band of skylights near its peak, under a deep blue sky, with the red sandstone office wing at its edge; no people in frame. Slide text: In Clark County, cannabis rules can reach the magazine. Clark County Government Center, 2011. County papers list magazines and consultants as support businesses.

A crop of Clark County's support business instructions: any person whose business provides ancillary support to cannabis establishments or the industry must apply for a county business license; such businesses include cannabis-related media outlets (magazines and other publications), cannabis business consulting and medical cannabis patient consulting. Slide text: Magazines are on the list. The county's support business packet lists "magazines and other publications" and business and patient consultants. The list is open-ended.

A crop of a 2022 Clark County bill, section 8.65.110: item 3, more than fifty percent of the business's total annual revenue within Clark County comes from cannabis products or services, then a list of support services beginning with security services and consulting services. Slide text: The code adds a revenue test. County code defines a support business as one earning over half its Clark County revenue from cannabis work. Consulting is on its list. Media is not named.

A crop of Clark County's support business instructions: once public safety inspections are done and agencies have signed off, the Department schedules a Code Conference with the applicant to review County Code requirements for the cannabis support business. Slide text: A code conference is last. After safety inspections and agency sign-offs, the county schedules a code conference to review the county code rules that may affect the support business.

A crop of a 2022 Clark County bill, section 8.65.160, Duties of licensee, with underlined added words extending the duties to holders of an adult-use cannabis support business license. Slide text: Since 2022, support licensees share the duties. An amendment approved December 20, 2022 added support business license holders to the chapter's duties section.

A crop of a 2020 Clark County bill, section 8.65.190, Signs and advertising: an adult-use cannabis establishment shall not use misleading advertising or advertising material that has not been approved by the department, with older state agency wording struck out. Slide text: Establishment ads get vetted. County code says a cannabis establishment shall not use advertising material the county department has not approved. The rule is written for the establishment.

A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678B.520, paragraph (b): an establishment shall not advertise in any publication or on radio, television or any other medium if 30 percent or more of the audience is reasonably expected to be under 21. Slide text: State law: no ads where 30 percent are under 21. Nevada bars a cannabis establishment from advertising in any publication or medium whose audience is reasonably expected to be 30 percent or more under 21.

A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678B.520, subsection 13: local governments may adopt stricter cannabis advertising ordinances on signs and on handbills, pamphlets and cards, excluding an advertisement in a newspaper of general circulation, trade publication or other print media. Slide text: Local limits on handouts stop at print media. Local governments may be stricter than the state on signs and handouts. The handout power excludes ads in newspapers, trade publications and other print media.

A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678B.530, subsection 2: a local government shall not regulate the content of an advertisement for the sale of cannabis unless it adopts an ordinance setting forth such regulations. Slide text: Ad content rules need an ordinance. Nevada says a local government may not regulate the content of a cannabis sale ad unless it adopts an ordinance setting out those rules.

The Las Vegas Convention Center facade in 2008: a pale wall with the center's name in large letters, flagpoles, trees and a fenced forecourt under a blue sky; no people close enough to recognize. Slide text: MJBizCon meets on unincorporated county land. The county says the convention center is unincorporated. MJBizCon's Dec. 1 program listed First Amendment issues in cannabis marketing.

posts.summary: Much of the United States draws the edge of the beach from tide tables. Hawaiʻi draws it where the winter waves stop. Seven court rulings, two lava flows and one planted hedge show how that line was set, fought over and written into law.

slides.alt: An old color photo of a curved beach of dark sand under a crowd of tall, leaning coconut palms, with white waves rolling in and two tiny people near the water.
A long two-story stone building with arched windows and a square clock tower, behind tall palm trees and a lawn, with a gold and black statue on a pedestal in front.
A wide slope of black sand runs across the photo, with white foamy surf washing over its lower half and a man standing ankle deep near the far end, below a row of palm trunks.

A black and white line map of a curved bay. Dashed and dotted lines marked 1915, 1940, 1968 and 1972 shorelines step inland toward a road, and a straight dashed line offshore is labeled centerline breakwater.
slides.credit: Source: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 1973

onScreen: Where a Hawaiʻi beach ends. In Hawaiʻi the public shore runs up to the highest reach of the winter waves, shown by plants or a line of debris.
1968: the court read three Hawaiian words. Two 1866 royal patents ran "ma ke kai," along the sea. The court held that means the upper reach of the waves, not a tide table.
1973: at Kaimū, the plants won. Where a beach shows a debris line and a vegetation line farther inland, the court presumed the year's highest waves reach the plants.
The shore kept moving. The Corps of Engineers mapped Kaimū's shoreline moving inland from about 1915 to 1972, about 170 feet in 57 years.
1977: new land from lava is public. After the 1955 eruption added land at Kehena, the court held that lava land vests in the people of Hawaiʻi. Shown: 1990 lava at Kalapana.
Planted naupaka does not count. In 2006 and 2014 the court put the shoreline at the plants or the debris, whichever is farther inland, and ruled out planted shrubs.
Most of the measured shore is eroding. USGS found a long-term erosion trend at 70 percent of points on Kauaʻi, Oʻahu and Maui. In 2020 the legislature set setbacks at no less than 40 feet.

posts.title: Total THC: the one word that moves the hemp line
posts.summary: The 2025 hemp law counts the acid form of THC. Here is what the text says, why most of it waits until December 11, 2026, and what no agency has published yet.

slides.alt: Close photo of the flowering top of a female cannabis plant: a dense green flower cluster with curling pale orange hairs, its leaves and bracts dusted with tiny white glands (trichomes), with saw-edged leaves around it. Slide text: Hemp's new test counts the acid. Cannabis sativa makes THC mostly as an acid, THCA. After December 11, 2026, the federal hemp test counts it.

A column of the Federal Register, April 28, 2026, quoting the 2018 definition: the plant Cannabis sativa L. with a delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis. Slide text: 2018: the test named delta-9 only. Hemp was cannabis with no more than 0.3 percent delta-9 THC, dry weight. DEA quotes that definition in its April 2026 order.

A screenshot of a 2016 journal abstract on PubMed Central: these cannabinoids do not occur in significant concentrations in cannabis but can be formed by decarboxylation of their corresponding acids, the predominant cannabinoids in the plant. Slide text: The plant makes the acid form. Researchers call the acids "the predominant cannabinoids in the plant." THCA carries one extra carboxyl group that THC lacks.
slides.credit: Source: Wang et al. 2016 (PMC), CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: A screenshot of a 2016 journal abstract on PubMed Central: the rate constants for THCA-A were twice those of CBDA and CBGA, and decarboxylation of THCA-A was forthright with no side reactions or by-products. Slide text: Heat turns THCA into THC. In a lab oven at 110 C, THCA fell as THC rose. The study reports conversion "with no side reactions or by-products."
slides.credit: Source: Wang et al. 2016 (PMC), CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 558: the new definition of hemp with a total tetrahydrocannabinols concentration, including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis. Slide text: 2025: total THC, acid included. The new definition counts "total tetrahydrocannabinols concentration (including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid)" at 0.3 percent or less.

A crop of Public Law 119-103, page 140 Stat. 1003: section 2019, Section 781 Extension, limiting the 2025 hemp amendments until December 11, 2026. Slide text: But not before December 11. A September 2026 law held most of the rewrite back. Until December 11, 2026, only the ban on cannabinoids the plant cannot make applies.

A Federal Register footnote from April 28, 2026: as of November 12, 2026, the hemp definition is revised to refer to total tetrahydrocannabinols including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, citing Public Law 119-37, section 781. Slide text: Even DEA's order said November 12. DEA's April 2026 order gave November 12 for the total THC test. Congress moved that step to December 11 in September.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 560: paragraph (3), directing FDA to publish within 90 days lists of cannabinoids the plant can naturally produce and THC-class cannabinoids that occur naturally. Slide text: Still open: FDA's lists, and Congress. FDA's cannabinoid lists were due within 90 days. As of Nov. 11, 2026, none is in the Federal Register. Check GovInfo before relying on a date.

posts.title: Every regulated cannabis plant in Nevada gets a data double
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. Nevada's licensed cannabis market follows each plant twice: once in the grow room and once in a state tracking system. This part covers what the rules require a licensee to log, move, test and count.

slides.alt: Close view of a Cannabis sativa stem with clusters of small pale green male flowers and serrated leaves, against a blue sky, in the botanical garden of the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany; no people, tags or products in frame. Slide text: Every regulated plant in Nevada gets a data double. In Nevada's licensed market, each plant also lives as entries in one state system.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678A.050: batch number means a unique numeric or alphanumeric identifier assigned to a batch by a cannabis establishment when the batch is planted. Slide text: The first ID comes at planting. Nevada defines a batch number as a unique code a licensee assigns to a batch of plants when the batch is planted.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678B.217: a cannabis establishment shall use the seed-to-sale tracking system managed by the Board's independent contractor, connect through its application programming interface, pay its fees, and ensure cannabis is tagged as required. Slide text: One state system, one API, and tags. Licensees must use the tracking system run by the Board's chosen contractor, connect through its API, pay its fees and tag cannabis as required.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678D.020, subsection 10: after receipt, the receiving cannabis establishment shall confirm the products are as described in the transportation manifest and separately document any differences in quantity in the seed-to-sale tracking system. Slide text: A transfer is checked at both ends. The receiving business confirms the load matches the manifest and logs any quantity difference in the tracking system.

A crop of the Nevada Administrative Code, section 678B.214, subsection 8: maintain a seed-to-sale tracking system, reconcile raw material to finished product for each job, and provide quarterly physical inventory counts by persons independent of the manufacturing process, with significant variances reported to the Executive Director. Slide text: Four counts a year, by independent staff. Quarterly physical counts by people outside production are reconciled to the perpetual inventory. Significant variances go to the Executive Director.

A crop of a Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board table, the Entry Error row: used only for data entry mistakes, such as transposed numbers or accidental extra digits; must not be used to correct sales-related errors; check marks for all four license types. Slide text: Fixes need a named reason. The Board's 2025 list of adjustment reasons limits Entry Error to typos, such as transposed numbers. It may not be used to fix sales errors.

A crop of Nevada Legislative Auditor report LA20-05, page 7: auditors compared tax returns of 10 cultivators and 5 dispensaries with tracking data for January to June 2018; data did not agree about 70 percent of the time for wholesale returns, and about 57 and 60 percent for retail and sales tax returns. Slide text: In 2018, the data and tax returns disagreed. State auditors found about 70 percent of cultivators' wholesale returns did not match.

A crop of a Nevada Department of Taxation page: the fair market value at wholesale effective October 1, 2026, including small bud 729 dollars a pound, flower 1,037 dollars, trim 150 dollars and pre-roll 1,134 dollars, calculated from cultivator transactions in the seed-to-sale tracking system from June 1 to August 31, 2026. Slide text: The logs now help set a tax value. Taxation set the October 2026 flower value at $1,037 a pound from transactions logged in the state system.

A crop of the Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board Item Catalog FAQ, page 2: the catalog may list Metrc package ID numbers, unique identifiers assigned to each product package and shown on the label, and a certificate of analysis linked to the specific package. Slide text: Shoppers see a slice of the data. The state's public Item Catalog shows package ID numbers and a lab certificate linked to each package, for items sold in the last 180 days.
slides.credit: Source: Nevada CCB, Item Catalog FAQ

slides.alt: A crop of Nevada Revised Statutes 678A.455: a Board agent may issue a hold order only under regulations the Board adopts; the regulations must limit hold orders to products that fail a requirement and are a substantial hazard, require notice, and end the hold within 30 days unless extended after a hearing. Slide text: Still open: the hold-order rules. A 2025 law lets Board agents hold hazardous cannabis; past 30 days needs a Board order. The detailed rules it calls for are only proposed.

posts.title: Why an undersea cable needs a license to land in Hawaiʻi
posts.summary: In 1902 the first cable across the Pacific came ashore in Honolulu on a president's permission. A standoff off Miami in 1920 turned that permission into law. The same law, with rules that took effect in July 2026, decides every cable that lands on Oʻahu.

slides.alt: A grainy old photo of calm water filled with rowboats and canoes, a man standing in a canoe in front, and a crowd on a tree-lined beach behind.

Printed heading Terms and Conditions Which the Commercial Pacific Cable Company Has Offered to Accept, above text naming Mr. Mackay's letter of September 24, 1901, to Hon. John Hay, Secretary of State.
Printed court text saying the cable ship Colonia was stopped off Miami by United States destroyers and warned not to lay her cable within three miles of Miami Beach, where naval forces stood by.

Printed text of Chapter 12, An Act Relating to the landing and operation of submarine cables in the United States, saying no person shall land or operate a submarine cable without a written license from the President.

Printed rule text headed section 1.70002 General requirements: a cable landing license must be obtained before landing a cable that connects Alaska, Hawaii or U.S. territories with a foreign country, the continental United States or each other.

Typed government text headed Conditions, granting a petition filed on behalf of the Committee and conditioning the grant on Hawaiki Submarine Cable USA and BW Digital keeping a 2025 commitment letter and a 2022 agreement.

onScreen: Why an undersea cable needs a license to land in Hawaiʻi. At the end of 1902 the first cable across the Pacific came ashore at Waikīkī, on a president's permission.
Before any law, the terms came in a letter. In 1901 John W. Mackay asked the Secretary of State on what terms his cable could land, and offered eleven.
1920: destroyers stopped a cable off Miami. The Navy kept Western Union's cable three miles out. In 1921 an appeals court said the power to allow landings belongs to Congress.
1921: Congress wrote six short sections. No one may land an undersea cable without a written license from the President. That covers a cable joining Hawaiʻi to the mainland.
July 2026: the rules name Hawaiʻi. FCC rules now require a license for any cable linking Hawaii with a foreign country, the mainland or a U.S. territory.
Security agencies read the ownership chart. In 2025 the FCC added a Tonga branch to the Hawaiki cable, which lands at Kapolei, only on conditions a committee of agencies set.
Next: a new landing station on Oʻahu. The FCC licensed Google's Bulikula cable in December 2025. A Google company will build and own its new Oʻahu station.

onScreen: Paradise in Limbo Hawaii's Cannabis Journey and the Road That Keeps Closing
In 2000, Governor Ben Cayetano signed Act 228 into law. The move made Hawaii the first state in the nation to legalize medical cannabis through its legislature, rather than a ballot initiative.
In 2015, the legislature passed Act 241, creating the Medical Cannabis Dispensary Program. The law created a tightly controlled market: eight dispensary licenses.
Hawaii's dispensaries, in dates. Feb. 1, 2017: First production centers cleared to grow; Aug. 8, 2017: First dispensary cleared to sell; Dec. 23, 2025: 24 retail locations open.
Registered patients peaked at 35,444 in August 2021. By November 2024 the count was 30,035, down more than 15 percent, the Legislature found in 2025.
Speaker Nakamura confirmed that neither HB 1624 nor HB 1625 had enough support to advance. SB 2421, the Senate companion to HB 1625, was heard in committee on February 17, 2026 and did not advance.
Hawaii law defines marijuana as “any part of the plant (genus) cannabis.” HRS 712-1240. Shown: a pressed Cannabis sativa specimen.
Possession of three grams or less is a civil violation with a $130 fine. Possession of more than three grams is a petty misdemeanor under HRS 712-1249.
Federal law now treats marijuana under a state medical license as Schedule III. The federal order took effect April 28, 2026. Other marijuana remains Schedule I. Current as of November 12, 2026.

onScreen: December, Seeds and the Home Grower What the federal hemp change says about seeds.
Two dates, not one. November 12, 2026 starts the first exclusion. December 11, 2026 starts the rest. Until then the 2018 wording applies, unless Congress acts again.
2018: seeds counted as hemp. Hemp includes “the seeds thereof” at 0.3 percent delta-9 THC, dry weight. The text does not say whose THC counts for a seed.
The new test looks at the plant. Viable seeds from a plant over 0.3 percent total THC, counting THCA, are not hemp. Pub. L. 119-37, section 781.
Industrial hemp seed stays hemp. Seed grown for grain, oil, cake, nut or hull, for microgreens, or made only for those uses is inside the industrial hemp definition.
Excluded products fall back under the CSA. The Congressional Research Service says they “would instead be subject to regulation under the CSA as marijuana.”
Shipping protections name hemp. Section 10114 and section 737 cover hemp grown under farm bill programs. They do not address seeds excluded from hemp.
Hawaii already bars selling viable hemp seeds. Rule 11-37-3 allows sales only to a USDA-licensed hemp producer or a permitted hemp processor. DOH lists all viable hemp seeds as prohibited.
State law counts seeds as marijuana. HRS 712-1240 defines marijuana to include the seeds. Its hemp exceptions turn on who holds the hemp or on a finished product.
Hawaii's hemp chapter has an end date. The code's notes repeal chapter 328G on July 1, 2027, unless the legislature acts.
The patient statute does not name seeds. OMCCR lists three sources: a licensed dispensary, personal growing, a registered caregiver. Its guidance does not mention seeds.

posts.title: When US law banned ceremony: the 1883 Code of Indian Offenses
posts.summary: In 1883 the Sun Dance was banned not by an act of Congress but by an eight-page set of rules from the Interior Department, and Indian judges were told to enforce it. onScreen: When US law banned ceremony. In 1883 an Interior Department rule made the sun dance an "Indian offense," punished by the loss of rations.
It began with a letter. In December 1882 Interior Secretary Henry M. Teller asked for rules to "restrict and ultimately abolish" the dances and the work of medicine men.
A jail term with no fixed end. Rule 6 jailed a medicine man for at least ten days, or until he promised, "approved by the agent," to "forever abandon" his practices.
1888: a judge upheld the court. No act of Congress created it. Judge Matthew Deady called the courts "mere educational and disciplinary instrumentalities."
1904: "so-called religious ceremonies." The rewritten rules named the sun dance "and all other similar dances and so-called religious ceremonies" as "Indian offenses."
1978: Congress set a policy. It admitted ceremonies had been "in a few instances banned." In 1988 the Supreme Court found the act gave no right to sue.
The court still sits. In 2022 the Supreme Court counted five CFR courts serving 16 tribes. Their code today has no religious offenses.

posts.title: Nevada reserved ten lounge licenses for social equity. Then the process kept going.
posts.summary: A 2021 law set aside 10 cannabis lounge licenses for people harmed by past drug laws. Here is what the law said, how the state picked the applicants, what a 2024 audit found, and where the 10 licenses stood in October 2026.

slides.alt: The Nevada State Legislature building in Carson City, a pale stone building with a small dome and columned entrance, flags flying, snow on the lawns and bare trees in front; no people in frame. Slide text: Nevada reserved ten lounge licenses for social equity. The Legislature in Carson City, 2009. In 2021, lawmakers set aside at least 10 of the first 20 independent lounge licenses. Then the process kept going.

A crop of the enrolled text of Nevada Assembly Bill 341, page 8: section 12.4 in blue type, capping independent cannabis consumption lounge licenses at 20 and requiring at least 10 of the first 20 to go to social equity applicants. Slide text: The law: at least 10 of the first 20. AB 341 capped licenses for independent lounges, those not attached to a store, at 20. At least 10 of the first 20 must go to social equity applicants.

A crop of Nevada Cannabis Compliance Regulation 5.055, Selection of social equity applicants: at least 51 percent ownership, five years in a census tract with an Area Deprivation Index decile of 7 or higher and an incarceration rate in the 90th percentile, a cannabis conviction of the applicant or a parent, sibling or child, and a 75 percent fee reduction. Slide text: Eligibility ran on an address. A 51 percent owner needed five years in a census tract high on deprivation and incarceration scores, and a cannabis conviction, their own or a close relative's.

A crop of a Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board release of November 23, 2022: a paragraph on the initial review of lounge applications and a table of complete applications, total 99, retail 20, independent 49, independent as a social equity applicant 30. Slide text: 99 complete applications. 30 came from social equity applicants. The window ran October 14 to 27, 2022. On November 30, a computerized random number selector drew 10 of the 30.

A crop of the table Results From Internal Audit from a Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board release of July 2, 2024: the header and rows 1 to 10, the applications drawn in 2022, numbered with no names. Six rows carry red crosses on the incarceration rate (84th, 67th, 42nd, 77th, 51st and 86th percentiles); four carry green checks; all ten pass the Area Deprivation Index test. Slide text: 2024: six of the ten were not eligible. An audit begun in January 2024 found the Opportunity Atlas results miscalculated in 6 of the 10 drawn.
slides.credit: Source: NV CCB audit table, July 2, 2024

slides.alt: A crop of a Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board release of July 2, 2024: investigators found the Opportunity Atlas results were miscalculated in 6 of the 10 drawn applications, requested the residential addresses all 30 applicants relied on, and found at least 8 of the 20 undrawn applicants met the residency requirement on both atlases at the time of the licensing round. Slide text: The Board asked all 30 for their addresses. At least 8 of the 20 undrawn applicants gave addresses that met both tests at the time of the 2022 round.

A crop of a Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board release of August 22, 2024: an internal audit found 6 previously selected applicants ineligible, the Board contacted 8 previously undrawn applicants in July and all 8 opted in, and the Board is returning the $2,500 application fee to social equity applicants not proceeding. Slide text: A second draw filled the six places. All 8 eligible applicants opted in, and six won prospective licenses in August 2024. The Board said it would return the $2,500 fee to those not proceeding.

A crop of the Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board minutes of May 15, 2025, agenda item III, Consideration of Approval for a Conditional License for a Cannabis Consumption Lounge: staff noted item A was the first social equity applicant to appear before the Board and that each applicant must still complete local approvals and final inspection before opening. Slide text: May 2025: first social equity conditional license. Two more followed in 2025. Each still needs local approval and a final inspection to open.

A screenshot of the Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board statistics page, October 2026, section Licensed Adult-Use Cannabis Establishments: 103 cultivation facilities, 82 production facilities, 8 independent testing laboratories, 3 lounge facilities, 106 retail cannabis stores and 42 distributors. Slide text: October 2026: three lounges open statewide. Board documents tie all three active lounge licenses to retail stores. None went to a social equity applicant.

A bar chart on graph paper titled Nevada's social equity lounge applications, by stage: 30 complete applications, November 2022; 10 drawn, November 30, 2022; 6 drawn then found not eligible, July 2, 2024; 8 undrawn found eligible on recheck, July 2, 2024; 6 picked in the second draw, August 22, 2024; 3 conditional licenses, May to September 2025; 0 active lounge licenses, October 2026. Slide text: 30 applications. No social equity lounge open yet. Three hold conditional licenses. Ask for the count and date at each stage.

posts.title: The ship named in the law
posts.summary: In 1900 Congress named five sailing ships when it brought federal shipping rules to Hawaiʻi. One of them, the Falls of Clyde, sat in Honolulu Harbor until 2025. The law it was named in still decides which ships may carry cargo between the islands and the rest of the country.

onScreen: The ship named in the law. In 1900 Congress named the Falls of Clyde in the act that put shipping between Hawaiʻi and the mainland under the coastwise laws.
1900: section 98 named five ships. It gave them American registers and put trade between the islands and the rest of the country under the coasting laws.
1920: the Jones Act. Senator Wesley Jones changed the cargo rule in section 27 so it covered goods moving by land and water between American points.
Almost everything comes by sea. More than 90 percent of the goods imported into Hawaiʻi enter through Honolulu Harbor, the state says.
American-built ships cost more. A U.S.-built ship cost 1.2 times a foreign one in 1922. By 2019 a tanker was about four times the world price.
No American livestock ships. So Hawaiʻi calves reach the mainland by air or in containers on Jones Act ships, the ranchers' council says.
One cruise line's exception. A 2003 law let Norwegian Cruise Line finish ships abroad and sail them between the islands under the U.S. flag.
The law still stands. In January 2026 a federal judge dismissed a Kauaʻi distillery's challenge. Bills to exempt Hawaiʻi have not left committee.

glossary.definition: The Jones Act is the common name for a 1920 shipping rule, which says that goods moving by water from one American place to another must travel on ships that are American-built, American-owned and mostly American-crewed

posts.title: When Two Versions of the Law Disagree
posts.summary: For nearly a century the Hawaiian Kingdom and then the Territory published their laws twice, once in Hawaiian and once in English. When the two texts said different things, someone had to decide which one was the law. The answer changed in 1859, and the Legislature is still arguing about it.

slides.alt: A black-and-white photograph from about 1870 of Aliʻiōlani Hale in Honolulu, a two-story stone government building with a clock tower and a tall flagpole in an open yard. It was the Kingdom government building that later housed its Legislature and Supreme Court.
slides.credit: Photo: HABS / Hawaii State Archives, PD
slides.url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_EXTERIOR_VIEW_OF_NORTHEAST_(FRONT)_ELEVATION_FROM_EAST_(Photo_ca_1870,_from_original_in_Hawaii_State_Arvhices).__Photocopy_1966_-_Aliiolani_Hale,_463_King_Street,_Honolulu,_HABS_HI,2-HONLU,3-21.tif (HABS HI-2-HONLU-3-21, 1966 photocopy of a c. 1870 print in the Hawaii State Archives; cropped to the print)

slides.alt: Page 6 of the Compiler's Preface to the 1846 Statute Laws, in old printed type. It says the code went to the king's cabinet for discussion, then to the Rev. William Richards for faithful translation into the native language, then to both houses for three readings, debated section by section.

Page 259 of volume 1 of the Hawaiian Reports, headed 1856, Hardy vs. Ruggles, in old printed type. The lines read that where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian, the latter must govern, because it is the language of the legislators of the country.

Page 367 of the 1859 Civil Code, Chapter XLI, General Provisions, in old printed type. Section 1493 says that if a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian versions of any part of the Code, the English version shall be held binding. The page ends with the approval of May 17, 1859, signed Kamehameha.

Four lines of old printed type from the same page of Hardy v. Ruggles. They read that the English and Hawaiian may often be used to help and explain each other where the meaning is obscure, or the contradiction slight, but where the omission in the Hawaiian is clear, it is impossible to reconcile them.

A printed act headed An Act for the Construction of Statutes Where the English and Hawaiian Versions Do Not Agree. Its one section says that whenever a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian version of any of the laws of the Kingdom, which have been, or may hereafter be enacted, the English version shall be held binding. Approved January 10, 1865, signed Kamehameha R.
slides.credit: Source: Laws of 1864 to 1865, p. 68, PD

slides.alt: A 1943 session-law page headed Promulgation of Laws. Act 218 rewrites the rule so that the secretary of the Territory publishes the laws once in the English language in a Honolulu daily newspaper. The Hawaiian-language publication is gone from the text.

Two crops of a 1979 session-law page, Act 97, S.B. No. 45. It rewrites section 1-13: English and Hawaiian are the official languages of Hawaii; where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian version of any state law, the English version shall be held binding; Hawaiian shall not be required for public acts and transactions.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 16, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined new text adds a proviso to section 1-13: if a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian and its English version was translated from it, and the law has not been subsequently amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English, the Hawaiian version shall be held binding.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 109, S.D. 2, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined text adds the same proviso for laws originally drafted in Hawaiian and not later amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English. Its last line reads: This Act shall take effect on July 1, 3000.

A typed bill page, H.B. No. 2433, H.D. 1, S.D. 1, with numbered lines. The sentence making the English version binding is struck through. New underlined text gives priority to the language that aligns with the intent of the legislature as evidenced by legislative history, context and purpose. The last line sets the effective date at March 22, 2075.

Seven lines of old printed type from page 480 of volume 8 of the Hawaiian Reports, April 1892, In re Ross. They read that the English version shall be held binding, that the two versions constitute but one act, that there is no dual legislation, and that as a rule one version is the translation of the other.

The top of page 69 of volume 2 of the Hawaiian Reports, 1858, Levi Haalelea v. Daniel Montgomery, in old printed type. It reads that the deed is a printed formula in two languages, that the English version of this formula is, of course, the original, and the Hawaiian merely a translation.

onScreen: When Two Versions of the Law Disagree The Hawaiian Kingdom governed through laws published in Hawaiian and English.

A law was drafted in one language and translated into the other. In 1845 and 1846, Attorney General John Ricord drafted the new laws in English. William Richards translated them into Hawaiian, and both houses gave each act three readings.

In Hardy v. Ruggles (1856), the Hawaiian Kingdom’s Supreme Court held that where the English and Hawaiian versions differ in a radical and irreconcilable way, the Hawaiian governs, “because it is the language of the legislators of the country.”
The 1859 Civil Code decided it the other way three years later.
Where wording was obscure or the contradiction slight, the Hawaiian and English could be used to help explain one another.
In 1865 the English rule was extended to every law of the Kingdom, both those already passed and those passed later.
From 1943 the Territory published its new laws in English only. When only one language is routinely produced, later researchers do not encounter two parallel witnesses.
HRS section 1-13 today:
A 2023 bill proposed Hawaiian priority when a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian. A House committee limited it to laws not later amended, codified or reenacted in English. It did not become law.
Senate Bill 109 carried the same approach into the 2025 to 2026 session, but it did not become law. A House draft set its effective date at July 1, 3000.
A 2026 draft looked to intent instead. House Bill 2433 would give priority to the version that matches the Legislature’s intent. The Senate draft’s effective date is March 22, 2075.
What We Actually Know
The durable technological lesson is narrower and stronger.

posts.title: The Observatory That Turned a Volcano into a Century-Long Signal
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. In 1912 a geologist began measuring Kīlauea every day and writing the numbers down. This part follows the logbooks, cellars, gas tubes and warnings of the observatory's first decades. It also follows the people who kept the measurements going when the founder was away.

slides.alt: Aerial photograph taken on May 8, 2018 of the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory's Okamura building and the Jaggar Museum on Uēkahuna Bluff, above the dark floor of Kīlauea's caldera. It opens the story with the observatory and the volcano in one frame, as the buildings stood just before the summit collapse.
slides.credit: Photo: J. Christensen, NPS, Public domain

slides.alt: a view straight down the six-meter borehole that houses HVO's UWE tiltmeter at the summit of Kīlauea, taken during releveling on July 2, 2024. It shows one of the instruments that produce the tilt signals the sentence is about; it is not the subject of the sentence itself.
slides.credit: Photo: M. Warren, USGS, Public domain

slides.alt: two HVO technicians install a solar-powered seismic station near the summit of Kīlauea in February 2008, with an antenna mast, solar panel and Mauna Loa in the background. It shows one sensor site and its radio link, a single part of the monitoring system the sentence describes.

Photograph pasted into HVO's 1912 logbook, dated January 25, 1912 and initialed by Jaggar: a dim view across Halemaʻumaʻu from the rim, with three figures at the lower right on the edge. It shows the rim vantage where the continuous study began; the people are not named in the book.

a row of paper-drum seismograph recorders in the Thomas A. Jaggar Museum, each labeled with a different HVO station name, photographed in 2010. It shows that the data are made by particular instruments at particular places; it is not the subject of the sentence itself.

Photograph from HVO's 1912 logbook, dated January 26, 1912 (nine days after the arrival the slide describes) and initialed by Jaggar: two men stand on the cracked lava crust of the crater floor near a steam vent, under the high crater wall. It shows the lava-lake setting where the surveying took place.

Photograph of the Volcano House hotel manager's room in the early 1900s, from a glass-plate negative at the Hawaiʻi State Archives: a man sits at a table in a room hung with dried leaf fringe and framed portraits, and the plate carries the caption 'Volcano House Manager's Room'. It shows the room of the hotel that Demosthenes Lycurgus operated; who the seated man is has not been confirmed.

Photograph taken May 28, 1912 inside Halemaʻumaʻu: two men stand on the lava floor beside a crate of sampling bottles, with tubing running to a steaming dome from which the gases were collected. USGS Professional Paper 1801 names the two men in its own photo of the same collection as Shepherd and Dodge; this plate's caption does not name them. It is the actual gas collection the sentence describes.
slides.credit: Photo: A. L. Day and E. S. Shepherd, PD
slides.url: https://archive.org/details/bulletinofgeolo241913geol (Bulletin of the Geological Society of America, vol. 24, 1913, plate 20; leaf 677)

slides.alt: 1912 photograph of the Whitney Laboratory of Seismology: a timber-beamed room with concrete piers carrying tall pendulum seismographs and their drums, with windows along one wall. It is the Whitney Vault named in the sentence; Wood is not pictured.
slides.credit: Photo: T. A. Jaggar, 1912, USGS, PD

slides.alt: Photograph from HVO's 1912 logbook, dated February 4, 1912 and initialed by Jaggar: the wooden Technology Station on Kīlauea's rim behind a picket fence, with a man standing in the doorway. It shows the first small building the observatory work grew from; the man is not named.

Photograph from HVO's 1912 logbook, dated February 16, 1912 and initialed by Jaggar: a plain wooden building frame under construction on open ground, with workers beside it. It shows the first permanent observatory building going up, the construction the card's funding row refers to.

two cylinders wrapped in paper seismograms, one covered in short spikes from an earthquake swarm and one with the dense bands of harmonic tremor, mounted on the wall of the Jaggar Museum at the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory. It shows what the paper era produced, ink traces on paper drums, not Wood’s arrival or the half million items themselves.

Photograph from June 6, 2024 of an HVO field engineer burying the cable for a new seismometer at a Kīlauea Southwest Rift Zone station that already carries GPS and high-resolution gas equipment, with solar panels and a radio dish beyond. It shows the three signal families the sentence names, earthquakes, deformation and gases, at one modern site; it does not show the early observers' instruments.
slides.credit: Photo: M. Warren, USGS, Public domain

slides.alt: Photograph from June 2018 of a temporary GPS station on the floor of Kīlauea's caldera: a yellow tripod carrying a GPS antenna, with a solar panel and radio telemetry, steaming crater wall behind. It shows the GPS tool in the sentence's list of later deformation systems, used to track the summit subsidence; it does not show Jaggar-era surveying.
slides.credit: Source: USGS Volcano Hazards Program, PD

slides.alt: Photograph of an HVO geochemist at the rim of Halemaʻumaʻu photographing an FTIR spectrometer on a tripod pointed into the gas-filled crater; the page dates the image to July 2016. It shows gas being measured at Kīlauea, the window the sentence adds. The geochemist is not named.
slides.credit: Source: USGS Volcano Hazards Program, PD

onScreen: The Observatory That Turned a Volcano into a Century-Long Signal A volcano does not announce an eruption in a language made for humans.
No single change means the same thing every time.
The technology of volcano monitoring is therefore not one heroic sensor. It is a system for making fallible observations comparable across time, and for deciding when a pattern justifies action.
On Kīlauea’s rim in 1912, the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory began continuous, systematic study of Hawaiian volcanic and earthquake activity. Jaggar is conventionally identified as its founder.

“A century of data” can sound like possession of the volcano’s whole history. It is a century-scale body of data made by particular institutions, instruments, categories, and decisions about what to measure.
Jaggar reached Hilo on January 17, 1912, traveled to Volcano House, and began surveying the lava lake that afternoon. But an observatory could not survive as one scientist looking into a crater.
Demosthenes Lycurgus, who operated Volcano House, led local fundraising. Hilo businesses contributed $1,785 toward construction.

Carnegie Laboratory director Arthur Day and E.S. Shepherd came to collect volcanic gases and remeasure temperatures. Dodge joined them in descending into Halemaʻumaʻu to obtain samples before the gases mixed with air.
Seismologist H.O. Wood arrived with Jaggar in June and put the mechanical instruments into operation in the Whitney Vault.

A monitoring institution emerged through collaboration among local supporters, field workers, assistants, outside laboratories, publication networks, and instruments, not through a lone moment of invention.

and still never receiving the project file behind it.
The brand may receive a finished MP4, PDF or PNG that looks completely done.
The editable project file is a different thing:

Linked footage, fonts, links and license files can sit outside the final export,

Before delivery, ask exactly what the next person can open, change and reuse.

onScreen: The year Hawaii rewrote the 329 card Acts 46, 241 and 269 of 2025: certification, telehealth, fees, caregivers and hemp sellers.
Three laws in 2025 Act 46 was approved May 14. Act 241 followed on June 27, and Act 269 on July 2.
A new way to qualify A primary treating medical provider can certify a condition not on the debilitating list. A hospice provider can certify hospice care.
Who counts as a primary treating provider A Hawaii physician or APRN, licensed in the state, primarily responsible for your treatment and ongoing care.
Telehealth is allowed No initial in-person visit is required. The provider must be in Hawaii and meet the same standard of care. OMCCR's guidance starts September 18, 2025.
A cap on certification fees No more than three times the Department's registration fee. OMCCR's fee page caps it at $105 for one year and $315 for three.
The Department can inspect files It may inspect the files behind a certification, and suspend or revoke a provider who refuses.
Caregivers can grow again Act 46 restored caregiver cultivation, retroactive to January 1, 2025. Fines can reach $5,000 per violation, and each day counts separately.
Five patients A caregiver may serve up to five patients. Each growing location may be used for not more than five patients.
A cultivator license starts in 2028 From January 1, 2028, Act 241 Part IV makes it unlawful for any person to cultivate cannabis without a Department license.
Hemp sellers must register Since January 1, 2026, hemp product retailers and distributors need a certificate: $50, valid five years. Topicals and tinctures are exempt.
What we know and what we do not
Education, not legal advice OMCCR's own guidance sheets say they do not replace legal advice, and neither does this. For your situation, ask a Hawaiʻi attorney.

onScreen: The FTC's Fortnite case didn't turn on whether players saw buttons. It turned on what the buttons made likely.
The order: $245 million for refunds, express consent before charges, and no account lockouts for disputing a charge. By mid-2025, nearly $200 million had gone out.
Design can obscure, subvert or impair choice. Not all influence is unlawful. All of it is worth examining.
A form is an interface. The Plain Writing Act puts part of the burden of understanding on the agency that wrote it.
Federal law counts the minutes you spend on a form as a cost, and lets you refuse a form with no valid control number.
Waiting is designed too: the median ER wait to see a provider rose 22 percent from 2003 to 2009, from 27 to 33 minutes.
Can the person see where they are, pause and come back? Federal digital teams wrote it into the playbook.

posts.title: The Gate That Thinks With the Tide
posts.summary: Heʻeia Fishpond is enclosed by a stone wall about 1.3 miles long, and its gates admit water and small fish while keeping grown fish home. Floods, mangrove, a fish die-off and a stream diversion broke that system. The studies and reports on its rebuilding show what the gates do, and what they still lack.

slides.alt: Looking across the shore toward Heʻeia Fishpond in Kāneʻohe Bay: the long, low line of the pond wall and its tree-covered stretches sit on calm water, with the green Koʻolau ridges rising behind in low light. It opens the story on the place itself, the pond named in the first sentence.

A published map from a 2019 study: the island of Oʻahu, then a satellite view of the Heʻeia land division outlined in yellow, with Heʻeia Stream drawn in blue from the Koʻolau ridge through the Hoi wetland to the pond, shaded red, at the edge of Kāneʻohe Bay. It shows where the fresh water comes from that mixes with the tide inside the pond.

Photos from a 2019 study of two gates at Heʻeia Fishpond, labeled Nui and Kahoʻokele: water rushes through a stone channel under a wooden frame, and a row of upright slats crosses a channel with calm water and mountains behind. These are mākāhā, the gates the slide names.

A grid of 24 blue scatter plots from a 2019 study, one row for each of six gates at Heʻeia Fishpond and one column each for spring flood, spring ebb, neap flood and neap ebb tides. Each plot shows how much water passed through that gate as the water level changed, logged every 20 seconds. It shows water moving through the openings; fish are not measured in this figure.

From a hillside of green shrubs at Heʻeia State Park, the long straight wall of Heʻeia Fishpond runs across calm blue water toward the Koʻolau mountains, January 2019. It shows the wall the slide says no source credits to one designer.

The middle section of the Heʻeia Fishpond wall in April 2010: a low wall of stacked blocks runs out across calm water, and on the near end white plastic buckets, boulders and broken coral are piled, ready to be moved. It shows material gathered by people for the wall.
