onScreen: The Gate That Thinks With the Tide The kuapā curves through Kāneʻohe Bay, built from stone and coral without becoming an impermeable barrier.
Inside, those flows make a brackish environment where limu and other food for fish can grow.
A mākāhā is often translated as a sluice gate.
The openings permit water and small fish to move. Juvenile fish can enter.
No reliable source identifies one person who designed Heʻeia Fishpond. Its wall is therefore not only a structure.
It is evidence of coordination: people selecting and moving material, reading a difficult coastal environment, organizing labor, maintaining a shared food system, and transferring knowledge.
The labor did not end when the wall was completed. Its productive capacity depends on continuous mālama: clearing channels, repairing storm damage, maintaining gates, observing fish and water,
controlling predators or invasive species, coordinating harvests, and caring for relationships upstream and downstream. Loko iʻa are living systems.

The physical system at Heʻeia makes that labor legible. Paepae o Heʻeia describes a wall built in compact layers that slow water loss, preserve a base level at low tide, and concentrate more exchange through seven mākāhā.
Together they help maintain brackish conditions favorable to limu and fish.

Restoration practitioners face watersheds altered by development, sediment and nutrient changes, invasive species, unreliable recruitment of juvenile fish, warmer water, storms, regulation, funding constraints, and the sheer physical demand of maintaining a coastal structure.

posts.title: Paid work is not automatically work made for hire
posts.summary: In 1985 a sculptor delivered a statue to a Washington charity, and four years later the Supreme Court ruled that the charity was not its author under the work-made-for-hire rule. A decade before the statue, a five-person firm had given NASA its best-loved logo. One federal rule decides who owns work like this, and payment is only one small part of it.

posts.title: The Lines That Changed the Land
posts.summary: Between 1846 and 1855, Hawaiʻi asked thousands of people to turn the land they lived on into written claims, testimony, surveys and awards. The laws, the award books and the surveyors' own accounts show how the lines were drawn, who drew them, and why courts still read them today.

slides.alt: A handwritten Land Commission award-book page of October 12, 1850: a pen-and-ink plat of a parcel with a creek along one edge, hachured hillside and neighboring-land names, the tail of a courses-and-distances description above it, a costs list and the commissioners' signatures below. It is an actual parcel made legible as a drawing, a description and a signed document, which is the sentence this story opens with.

Turner in July 1850: a description of a Honolulu lot that starts at the corner of Nuuanu and King Streets and runs by bearings and chain lengths to the point of commencement, with a hand-drawn plat showing the Bethel Chapel and neighboring lots beside it. It shows a boundary put into words, measured and drawn on one page.

onScreen: The Lines That Changed the Land Before land can be sold as a parcel, it must be made legible as one.

A boundary must be described in words, followed across the ground, measured, calculated, drawn, attached to a name or number, accepted by an institution, and preserved in a document another institution will recognize.
A claimant did not present land itself to the commission.
A boundary known through a stream, a wall, a planting area, a ridge, a neighboring holding, or the memory of people in a place could be restated as a sequence of courses and distances.
The description could be calculated, copied, mapped, indexed, compared, and carried into a later dispute.
The lines on a cadastral map therefore deserve to be read twice. First as measurements: carefully made descriptions that allowed a boundary to be found again.

Second as instruments: documents that could transfer, divide, mortgage, foreclose, and settle a claim without anyone returning to the ground the boundary describes. Educational information, not legal advice.

The First Amendment has been read to protect the content of belief. Substantive due process has been held to protect intimate decisions about body, family, and identity.

Stanley v. Georgia (1969) "If the First Amendment means anything, it means that a State has no business telling a man, sitting alone in his own house, what books he may read or what films he may watch."
The Glucksberg test has two parts. The interest must be "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition," and the Court requires a "careful description" of it.
Dobbs may be the most serious structural challenge. Dobbs (2022) overruled Roe and Casey. The article says cognitive liberty has not been recognized as a constitutional right in prior doctrine.
Smith: neutral, generally applicable laws Employment Division v. Smith held that the Free Exercise Clause does not require religious exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws.
Raich and the commerce power Raich is a significant obstacle to any facial challenge to the CSA on Commerce Clause grounds.
What we know: Psilocybin and psilocyn, compounds in mushrooms like this liberty cap, remain in Schedule I as of November 15, 2026 (21 CFR 1308.11(d)).
What we don't know: The article reports that no federal court has ruled on a cognitive liberty claim. It says a court's answer cannot be predicted.
Describe the interest before you argue for it. What exactly is the interest being claimed? Is there a history and tradition behind that exact interest? Does the science show it, or only suggest it?

posts.title: Who donates a brain, and who decides?
posts.summary: The law says a signed gift belongs to the person who signed it. The national brain bank network still asks the family to sign at the time of death. A medical examiner can keep a brain without asking anyone. This is the chain of consent behind a donated brain, read from the statute, the court opinions and the studies of the people who signed.

onScreen: Who donates a brain, and who decides? Illinois law says that once a donor signs, a person other than the donor "is barred from changing, amending, or revoking" the gift.
The brain banks still ask the family. The NIH brain bank network tells donors that "a consent form must be signed by the next of kin at the time of death."
A license sticker is not enough. The network's own answer: the sticker on a driver's license "does not give brain banks permission to receive a brain."
No signature? A ladder decides. Illinois lists 11 classes, from a health care agent and a spouse down to a close friend. No one lower may decide if someone higher can be reached.
Signed is not the same as done. At Rush in Chicago, most signers in two studies came to autopsy. Among African American signers, 53.4 percent did, as of 2012.
A coroner can keep the brain. In 2008 Ohio's top court held that families had no protected right in organs a coroner removed and kept for testing.
Sometimes it is one phone call. Asked by phone on the day of an autopsy, 69.7 percent of families said yes: 74.1 percent of White families and 57.0 percent of Black families.

posts.title: Partnership Ads and Spark Ads: two permission trails

posts.title: The hemp timeline: eight years and three laws
posts.summary: How federal hemp law got from the 2018 farm bill to December 11, 2026, told date by date from the enacted texts and the Federal Register.

slides.alt: Rows of young hemp plants, Cannabis sativa, set in white plastic mulch with grass between the rows and trees behind, on a Maryland farm. Slide text: Hemp law, 2018 to December 11. Hemp rows on a Maryland farm in a USDA photo from 2020. The federal rules for this crop have moved in dated steps since 2018.

A crop of Public Law 115-334, page 132 Stat. 5018: section 12619, Conforming Changes to Controlled Substances Act, adding that the term marihuana does not include hemp. Slide text: Dec. 20, 2018: hemp leaves the drug law. The 2018 farm bill defined hemp at 0.3 percent delta-9 THC and wrote that the term marihuana "does not include" hemp.

A crop of the first page of Public Law 119-37: An Act making continuing appropriations and extensions for fiscal year 2026, dated Nov. 12, 2025, H.R. 5371. Slide text: Nov. 12, 2025: a rewrite in a funding law. Public Law 119-37, a stopgap spending act, rewrote the hemp definition in section 781 of its agriculture division.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 558: the opening of section 781, effective 365 days after the enactment of this Act, amending section 297A of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946. Slide text: It set a one-year clock. Section 781 opens "Effective 365 days after the enactment of this Act." That pointed to November 12, 2026.

A crop of the first page of Public Law 119-103: An Act making continuing appropriations and extensions for fiscal year 2027, dated Sept. 2, 2026, H.R. 6500. posts.title: The Machine Inside the Mountain
posts.summary: Part 1 of 2. In 1913 a sugar company drove a tunnel under the Koʻolau Range to carry stream water across Oʻahu. The mountain answered with more water than anyone had measured. This part follows the building of the ditch and what it took from the streams.

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1916 photograph looking down a timbered tunnel in the Waiāhole project: curved wooden arch forms overhead, a plank wall on the right and narrow rail tracks on the floor leading into the dark. The report's own caption reads 'Portion of tunnel, showing forms for arch of tunnel roof' and does not say which tunnel or heading. It opens the story inside the mountain, on the machine itself.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: USGS map of the Waiāhole Ditch System: a blue dotted line starts at the Kahana tunnels in the windward valleys, runs south past Waikāne and Uwao tunnels and Gates 30 and 31, passes under the Koʻolau at the North Portal, comes out past Adit 8 and crosses central Oʻahu to Reservoir 155. Black outlines mark the Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole watersheds the ditch draws from.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of two large riveted steel pipes arching over a cut in a hillside at Waikakalaua Gulch, with a railway track running through the cut below. The report's caption calls them steel pipes crossing a branch of the Oahu Railway, the larger one the new 72-inch pipe. They are the part of the route where the conduit crosses a gulch instead of a tunnel or ditch.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: First page of Act 111, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi 1998, the law that let the state buy the Waiāhole water system. Section 2 opens: Water belongs to the people and the State should be the steward in managing and ensuring the allocation of this resource for the highest and best use in the public interest.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph of a worker in a hat standing before two concrete-framed gates with hand wheels above them, set into the mouth of a finished section of the conduit. The report captions it 'Gates at a section of finished conduit.' It shows the kind of gate the sentence means, the control that moves in minutes.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Printed paragraph from page 111 of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion: For the reasons fully explained below, we affirm in part and vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The caption of the opinion as printed on page 97 of the Hawaiʻi Reports: In the Matter of the Water Use Permit Applications ... for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing. No. 21309. Supreme Court of Hawaiʻi. Aug. 22, 2000.

Letterhead of the State of Hawaiʻi Commission on Water Resource Management, dated December 24, 1997. The letter tells the parties that the Commission's Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Decision and Order for the Waiāhole Ditch Combined Contested Case Hearing are enclosed: the decision the Supreme Court later reviewed.

Black-and-white 2019 photograph of two large siphon pipes crossing Kipapa Gulch side by side: on the left a newer siphon behind a concrete intake with a wooden screen, on the right the historic riveted-steel siphon behind a rusted grate. The survey caption says the historic one is no longer in use and the newer one is in use. It shows the fixed physical network of the Waiāhole Ditch carrying today's water through 1916-era works.

Lines of type from page 6 of Kluegel's 1916 report: the highest intake at 790 feet, and the length of the main tunnel through the Koolau Ridge, 14,567 feet, or 2.76 miles, with the North Portal at 752 feet and the South Portal at 724 feet. The usual facts, which the slide says are not the only questions.

Black-and-white 1916 photograph inside the main tunnel: a wall of dark rock with water jetting and spraying out of it into the bore, and two men with lanterns standing near the floor. The report's caption reads 'Water issuing from water-bearing rock in the main tunnel, 10,550 feet from the South Portal, March 23, 1915,' and explains that the lanterns are held by men beside a drill. It shows the mountain's own stored groundwater, the landscape process the tunnel tapped.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Black-and-white 1914 photograph of six tunnel workers in work clothes and caps standing together underground in front of a rock face, with a drill rig and air hose across the foreground. The report's caption reads 'Japanese professional tunnel men, Main Tunnel, July, 1914,' and its text credits them with most of the drilling and mucking. It puts the people who built the tunnel in the frame.
slides.credit: Photo: C. H. Kluegel report, 1916, PD

slides.alt: Paragraph from page 178 of a 1913 USGS report, written about 1911, before the ditch: Waiāhole Stream rises in springs about 1,000 feet above sea level, its flow is fairly constant, and a part of the water is used for irrigating rice and taro lands in the lower part of the valley.

Typed lines from page 3 of a 2025 Hawaiʻi Senate bill on the Waiāhole water system, listing who depends on it today: Aloun Farms, the Hawaii Agriculture Research Center, Larry Jefts Farm, Mililani Nursery, Mililani Agricultural Park, Sugarland Farms, Waiawa Nursery, Waikele Farms, livestock ranchers, Mililani Memorial Park and the Waiawa correctional facility.

A Parshall flume on the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-8): a concrete channel that narrows in the middle so one depth reading gives a flow rate, with smooth fast water and tall grass on the banks. By 2019 a laser sensor upstream had replaced it. It shows a gauge, the subject of the line.

Page 728 of a 1921 territorial Supreme Court opinion setting out the deals made before the tunnel was dug: a fifty-year lease of Kahana's surplus water from May 27, 1916, and a December 30, 1912 deed of water rights in Kahana, Waikāne and Waiāhole for $257,500, each subject to the valley residents' water for household use and irrigation.

The start of the conclusion of the 2000 Waiāhole opinion, page 189: For the reasons stated in this opinion, we vacate in part the Commission's decision and remand for additional findings and conclusions ... regarding the following, beginning with an interim instream flow standard for windward streams.

Faded photograph from a 1913 USGS paper, captioned Velocity-area gaging station, Waiāhole Stream: two men measure the stream by wading it, one seated in the water and one holding a rod, while men in hats watch from the grassy bank. A flow measurement, the thing the line says cannot decide allocation on its own.

A metal gate set into the concrete wall of the Waiāhole Ditch near Mililani, with a staff scale marked in one-foot steps and a narrow concrete footbridge at right, photographed for the National Park Service HAER survey in June 2019 (HAER HI-146-4). The 1916 machine still decides, gate by gate, where today's water goes.
slides.credit: Photo: David Franzen, HAER, Public domain

slides.alt: Line chart from the USGS low-flow study, Figure 34: daily water released at Gate 31 to Waiāhole Stream from January 1999 to late 2004, a jagged blue line mostly between 5 and 25 million gallons a day, above a flat pink line for the Commission's targeted restoration flow of 4, then 4.8 million gallons a day.

onScreen: The Machine Inside the Mountain Inside Oʻahu’s Koʻolau Mountains, the Waiāhole tunnel still helps decide where water goes.
The project therefore did not simply capture rainfall after it entered a ditch. It recruited an entire mountain watershed.
Intakes, tunnels, ditches, siphons, reservoirs, and gates turned flow into a controllable route.
Once farms, towns, ecosystems, and institutions depend on a route, infrastructure becomes governance.
A gate can change flow in minutes. Deciding the lawful and sustainable flow can take years.
In 2000, the Hawaiʻi Supreme Court affirmed part of the Commission on Water Resource Management’s decision, vacated part and sent issues back.
Waiāhole’s present consequence is therefore a continuing design problem: how should a fixed physical network serve changing public purposes?
Ask which landscape processes it recruited,
whose labor made it durable,
what uses it displaced,
which dependencies formed around it,
what the gauges can and cannot tell us,
and which past decision is hiding inside the present baseline.

posts.title: Finding a Certifying Provider in Hawaiʻi
posts.summary: A 329 card starts with a signed certification. Here is who may sign one, what the state's provider list does and does not promise, how the 2025 law opened first visits to telehealth, and what the visit may cost.

onScreen: Finding a certifying provider What to expect in Hawaiʻi, what the state does and does not vouch for, and five questions to ask.
Who can certify Physicians and APRNs can certify when they have a bona fide relationship with you. Hospice providers can certify hospice patients.
OMCCR lists but does not vouch The list is not exhaustive. The Department of Health does not endorse providers or guarantee the list, and encourages patients to research them.
Ask about cannabis education OMCCR’s patient page says meeting a provider who has completed medical cannabis education is advisable. Its specialist list was under development on October 11, 2026.
The first visit can be telehealth Act 241 says the relationship need not start with an in-person visit. OMCCR says telehealth certification has been allowed since September 18, 2025.
Telehealth has rules The provider must be physically in Hawaiʻi during the visit. Telehealth must meet the same standard of care as an in-person visit.
A form alone is not enough OMCCR says an online questionnaire alone does not meet the standard of care. Each patient must be assessed individually.
What a visit may include Providers told OMCCR what to expect: bring ID, medical files and your medication list; expect a history review and a check for drug interactions.
The fee has a cap A certifier’s fee may not exceed three times the state registration fee, $105 for a 1-year certification. Fees must be disclosed first.
Rules moved after September 2024 That month’s newsletter said telehealth was for renewals only. Act 241 and OMCCR’s September 2025 guidance now allow telehealth for first visits.

posts.title: Embed, host or repost? Big Buck Bunny on YouTube
posts.summary: A rabbit cartoon from Amsterdam was made to be shared, and its makers put it on YouTube themselves. That makes it a clean test case. Showing YouTube's player on a web page, holding the file and uploading a fresh copy look alike to a viewer. The license, YouTube's terms and the courts treat them as three separate acts.

slides.alt: A frame from Big Buck Bunny, taken at 1:15 from the Blender Foundation's own 1080p release file: the large gray cartoon rabbit smiles behind white flowers in a meadow. It is the free, Creative Commons licensed film the sentence names.

Page 8 of the Ninth Circuit's 2023 opinion in Hunley v. Instagram, cropped to the paragraph that ends: Importantly, the embedding website does not store a copy of the underlying image. It is the court's own statement that an embed is not a new copy.

The entrance of the Studio/K cinema in Amsterdam on April 10, 2008, the premiere night of Big Buck Bunny: a red carpet between chrome posts and red ropes, a tall white rabbit cutout by the doors and bicycles parked to the right. It is the launch of the 2008 release the sentence describes.
slides.credit: Photo: William Maanders, CC BY 3.0 NL

slides.alt: The license card from the film's closing credits, at 9:39: white capital letters on a streaked brown background read Licensed as Creative Commons Attribute 3.0, and below it, www.bigbuckbunny.org. It is the license notice the film itself carries.

Section 3, License Grant, of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: a worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive, perpetual license to reproduce the work and include it in collections. It is the clause that permits the broad reuse the sentence names.

The start of section 4(b) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code, the credit clause: anyone who distributes or performs the work must keep intact all copyright notices and give credit reasonable to the medium, beginning with the name of the original author. It is the attribution condition the sentence says must be followed.

The entrance of YouTube's headquarters at 901 Cherry Avenue in San Bruno, California, with a YouTube sign on a hedge-covered wall, photographed August 9, 2010. It is the company that hosts uploaded copies on its own servers, the host the sentence names. It does not show where any file is stored.

Page 9 of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Hunley v. Instagram: the host server can control whether embedding is available and can delete or replace the image, and the browser shows whatever the host server supplies. It is the court's account of an embed showing the host's own copy on another page.

Page 34 of the Ninth Circuit's opinion in Hunley v. Instagram, cropped to the passage that says BuzzFeed and Time embedded but did not store the underlying photographs, so they did not directly infringe. It is the court applying the point that an embed makes no new copy of the file.

A chart titled Each upload is a new file, with three boxes: the YouTube upload of May 29, 2008 (9:57, license in the description only), the 4K YouTube upload of Nov 10, 2014 (YouTube's CC BY label), and the same 4K version on Blender's PeerTube site, Oct 27, 2018 (license field Attribution). It shows one film as several separate uploaded files, as the sentence says a repost is.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from YouTube data

slides.alt: Paragraph 44 of the EU Court of Justice's 2018 Renckhoff judgment: posting a work on another website gives rise to a new communication, independent of the one first authorized, which may stay available after the author removes the original. It is the court's statement that a repost is a separate copy needing its own permission.

Section 4(a) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: you must include a copy of, or the web address for, this License with every copy of the work you distribute or perform. It is the license link the sentence says to keep with the file.

Section 3(b) of the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 legal code: an adaptation must clearly label that changes were made, for example with the line The original work has been modified. It is the modification note the sentence asks for. Captions and transcripts are not license terms and are not shown.

A chart titled Host, embed or repost, with three boxes. Host: the file is on YouTube's servers, allowed by the uploader's license to YouTube. Embed: the file stays on YouTube and the page holds code that calls the player, allowed by YouTube's Terms. Repost: a separate copy that may outlast the original, allowed for this film by CC BY 3.0 and its conditions. It lays out the route choice the sentence asks for.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from source data

slides.alt: Page 36 of the Second Circuit's April 2026 opinion in Richardson v. Townsquare Media, quoting the License to Other Users clause of YouTube's terms, which covers use only as enabled by a feature of the service, such as video playback or embeds. It is the permission that comes with the embed route.

Section 106 of Title 17 of the United States Code, Exclusive rights in copyrighted works, from the 2023 edition printed by the Government Publishing Office, cropped to the heading and the first three rights: to reproduce, to prepare derivative works and to distribute copies. These are the owner's rights that still apply when a file is not openly licensed.

posts.title: The per-container cap: how the new hemp law measures a package
posts.summary: The 2025 hemp law caps finished products at 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Here is the text, the definition of a container, the federal data on children that framed the debate, and what is still undecided.

slides.alt: Young hemp plants, Cannabis sativa, growing thickly in raised beds inside a plastic-covered high tunnel in Crawford County, Indiana, with a water tank behind; no people in frame. Slide text: The new hemp cap counts the package. Hemp in an Indiana high tunnel, June 2022. A 2025 law caps the THC in each package of finished products made from it.
slides.credit: Photo: B. O'Connor, USDA NRCS, PD

slides.alt: A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 559: clause (iv), excluding final hemp-derived cannabinoid products with greater than 0.4 milligrams combined total per container of total THC and similar-effect cannabinoids. Slide text: 0.4 milligrams per container. A final product is not hemp if its container holds over 0.4 mg combined of total THC and THC look-alikes, as HHS decides.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 560: the definition of container as the innermost wrapping, packaging or vessel in direct contact with the product, and the exclusion of bulk shipping containers. Slide text: The container is the innermost pack. The law names "a jar, bottle, bag, box, packet, can, carton, or cartridge." Bulk shipping boxes and outer wraps do not count.

A crop of Public Law 119-37, page 139 Stat. 559: intermediate products excluded above 0.3 percent combined total, and when marketed or sold as a final product or directly to an end consumer. Slide text: Ingredients get a different line. Intermediate products are limited to 0.3 percent combined, and may not be marketed or sold to an end consumer at all.

A crop of an FDA web page: national poison control centers received 2,362 exposure cases of delta-8 THC products from January 1, 2021 to February 28, 2022; 41 percent involved patients under 18; 82 percent of unintentional exposures affected children. Slide text: FDA's 2022 count: 41 percent were under 18. Poison centers took 2,362 delta-8 THC cases in 14 months. 41 percent involved people under 18. FDA notes these are self-reported calls.

onScreen: One elder's yes is not a community's yes In 2008 Suriname asked a human rights court whom to consult: the Saramaka captains, one captain or the Gaa'man. The court said the Saramaka decide.
Chosen by the people themselves In 2007 the UN adopted a declaration, 143 to 4. Peoples take part in decisions "through representatives chosen by themselves."
Four men gave DNA. Their leaders were avoided. After a 2010 genome study of four San men, the San wrote: "In Genomics research, our leaders were avoided."
Come in through the door The San Code of 2017 names the San Council to manage research. A San leader asked researchers to come through the door, not the window.
Two systems, two answers The office for 12 of 13 Wet'suwet'en houses opposed a gas pipeline. All five elected bands signed benefit deals. A court called the people "deeply divided."
Two peoples, one levy A government-led study found the Khoi and San hold the traditional knowledge of rooibos. Under a 2019 deal, processors pay them 1.5 percent of the farm gate price.
Where the yes gets checked The 143 Parties to the Nagoya Protocol must take steps so that traditional knowledge used there was obtained with community consent. The US is not a Party.

posts.title: Who Is Supposed to Supply What the Law Requires?
posts.summary: A man asks a judge for a lawyer. A clerk hands back divorce papers. A mother cannot pay $2 a page. Court rulings, rules and orders show who has been told to supply what the law demands.

Typed court text saying the cities estimated about 1,700 transferred cases, chose a proposal paying $17,500 a month, which works out to $10 per case for April 2012, and that this makes effective help virtually impossible.

Typed order text setting, from January 1, 2026, 47 felony case credits, 120 misdemeanor case credits and 250 commitment case credits a year for a full-time appointed attorney, with a phase-in of at least 10 percent a year.

A 1971 Supreme Court page head, Boddie v. Connecticut, 373, above a paragraph saying the clerk of the Superior Court returned the papers because no entry fee had been paid, and efforts to get a waiver were to no avail.

A page of a 1996 Supreme Court opinion, headed 108, M. L. B. v. S. L. J., listing $1,900 for the transcript at 950 pages at $2 per page, $438 for other documents, $4.36 for binders and $10 for mailing.

A paragraph of a 1974 Supreme Court opinion saying there is no equality of treatment merely by providing students with the same facilities, textbooks, teachers and curriculum, because students who do not understand English are foreclosed from any meaningful education.

Will Espero: a supporter votes yes. A champion builds coalitions and spends political capital. He chaired the 2015 conference committee that passed the dispensary bill, Act 241.
In 2024, the Hawaii Senate passed SB 3335 to legalize adult use. Two House committees amended it. It went no further.
In 2026, HB 1624 proposed a constitutional amendment for adult use. In February, Speaker Nadine Nakamura said neither House bill would move ahead.
In a survey of 1,009 people in Japan, 57.5% said legal adult use would not affect a visit to Hawaii. From a 2025 report for the Hawaii Department of Health.
Guam legalized adult use in April 2019. The same report found no significant rise or fall in visits from Japan or South Korea, using data through December 2020.
D.C. voters approved Initiative 71 in November 2014. Certified count: 115,050 for, 49,168 against. It legalized possessing small amounts for personal use.
Congress then barred D.C. from using its funds to go further. The March 2024 spending law says no D.C. funds may be used to enact a law that legalizes recreational use of a Schedule I drug.
Marijuana under a state medical license is now federal Schedule III. In effect April 28, 2026. Other marijuana stays Schedule I. Current as of Nov. 15, 2026.

posts.title: The Windbreak Decree
posts.summary: In 1958 the Netherlands exempted hemp grown as a windbreak from part of its drug law. The decree, the 1976 Opium Act, a 1999 rewrite and a 2019 experiment law show how one farm rule was named in court, narrowed, dropped and finally replaced.

onScreen: Nov 19, 1971: a defendant asked the prosecution's chemist whether he'd considered "the windbreak decree of 1958." The decree was real. The name was his.
Before 1976, Dutch law prohibited dried tops of flowering plants. A green seedling in a pot did not clearly fit. In May 1971, seedlings sold for a guilder each, opposite a police station.
The 1976 Act was signed by Health Minister Irene Vorrink first, Justice Minister Dries van Agt second. Its two lists sorted drugs by risk.
Nothing was legalized. Under article 11, 30 grams or less of hemp or hashish fell to the lowest tier: still an offense, but a minor one.
The new definition: every part of the plant except the seeds. The law remembered as tolerance brought the living plant inside it.
Tolerance came from prosecutors, not the Act. Their guidelines of October 1976 gave no priority to having drugs for personal use or to small soft-drug sales.

posts.title: "You have two strikes against you"
posts.summary: A master's thesis in anatomy and neurobiology took its title from a father's warning. This is the story of that sentence: the page it sits on, the women who said something like it long before, the school that granted the degree, and the honest answer the study gave when it put a hard question to data.

onScreen: Renters, HOAs and the patient gardener What Hawaii's lease, condo and planned community statutes say about medical cannabis. Education, not legal advice.
Chapter 329 speaks to landlords once. Section 329-125.5 bars refusing to lease to a patient for status alone, unless the landlord would lose a federal benefit.
The rental rule: section 521-39. A lease clause allowing eviction of a tenant with a valid 329 certificate is void, with one smoking exception.
The smoking exception has two parts. The lease must already allow eviction for tobacco smoking, and the cannabis must be smoked. Both must be true.
Association documents can switch it off. Section 521-39 does not apply where condominium or planned community documents prohibit the medical use of cannabis.
Condominiums: section 514B-113. Condo documents allowing listed discriminatory practices against a resident with a valid certificate are void, with the same smoking exception.
Planned communities: section 421J-16. Same wording for planned community associations. Both keep the duty to give reasonable accommodations to people with disabilities.

posts.summary: In May 2024 a ChatGPT voice called Sky was paused after Scarlett Johansson said it sounded like her. OpenAI said the voice belonged to a different actor. Both statements are public. What they leave open is an old question about who owns the sound of a person.

slides.alt: a hand holding a smartphone that shows a ChatGPT page, with a laptop behind it (photographer Jernej Furman, May 2023). It shows the product the Sky voice belonged to; it is not the Sky voice, ChatGPT’s voice mode or the 2024 pause.

Scarlett Johansson smiling at a microphone during a panel at San Diego Comic-Con, July 2013 (photographer Gage Skidmore). The sentence reports her statement that Sky sounded like her own voice; the photo shows her only and says nothing about OpenAI, Sky or the dispute.

the Pioneer Building in San Francisco’s Mission District, photographed in 2019 when it housed offices of OpenAI and Neuralink. It shows the company that made the voices; it is not Sky, ChatGPT or any voice track.

an empty dubbing booth with a microphone on a stand, a script stand and a monitor, photographed in 2008. It shows the kind of room where a professional voice actor works; it does not show or identify the actor behind Sky.

Sam Altman seated outdoors in a gray sweater, November 17, 2022 (Village Global). The sentence reports what Altman said about the casting of the Sky actor; the photo shows him only and is not tied to that statement.

a studio condenser microphone and pop filter lit against a dark background (photographer Dejan Krsmanovic, 2018). It shows the equipment of the voice work Johansson says she was asked to do; it is not the request, Johansson or OpenAI.

a 1920 photograph of young people crowded around an early radio set, several wearing earphones to listen. It shows listening to a voice that comes from a machine; it is not the 2024 demo and not Johansson.

Scarlett Johansson holding a microphone on stage at San Diego Comic-Con, July 20, 2019 (photographer Gage Skidmore; file re-saved at lower JPEG quality to stay under 8 MB). The card reports her statement that the May 2024 Sky demo sounded eerily like her own voice; the photo shows her only and says nothing about OpenAI, Sky or the dispute.

the office building at 1515 Third Street in San Francisco's Mission Bay, photographed June 15, 2025, which was OpenAI's headquarters at that time. It is not where the May 2024 announcement was made and does not show the voice or the pause; it stands only for the company named on the card.

a close-up of an Imperial “The Good Companion” typewriter. It stands for letters written on a client’s behalf; the attorneys’ letters are not shown here, and the photo is not connected to OpenAI or Sky.
a Kay Real Time Sona-Graph, an electronic sound spectrograph, showing a trace of speech on its screen. Instruments like it were used to analyze speech and voices; it is not tied to Sky or Johansson.

a dubbing studio vocal booth with a desk, microphone, headphones and monitor, and no one in it (photographer Tamirsofer, 2018). It shows the place where a voice belongs to the performer who speaks it; it does not show whose voice Sky is.

Portrait of Scarlett Johansson at a photocall on May 21, 2025 (photographer Harald Krichel). The sentence says OpenAI's account does not replace Johansson's own response; the photo shows her only and says nothing about Sky, OpenAI or the dispute.

a Voice-O-Graph disc, on which a person’s voice was cut in a booth, photographed by Dietmar Rabich in 2015. It shows a voice captured as an object apart from the speaker’s face or name; it is not a session contract.
the live room and control room of Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Alabama, photographed in 2025. It shows where a performer’s session is made and logged; it is not connected to OpenAI or Sky.

slides.alt: a vocal microphone behind a pop filter in a sound-treated booth, in black and white (photographer Tim Sheerman-Chase, 2012). It stands for the voice track and the person who speaks into it; it is not a picture of Sky, a performer or OpenAI.

posts.title: The Species Gap
posts.summary: What plant produced it? State cannabis law asks licensed laboratories to certify a great deal about a cannabis product, but arguably not the threshold question of what plant produced it.

slides.alt: Illustrative photo: a multi-bay PCR machine, an instrument that copies DNA for DNA-based species identification. It is not a laboratory named in the article; it stands for the molecular authentication the title proposes.

Illustrative photo: a closed wooden herbarium cabinet with specimen tags, at the Auckland Museum. It stands for the question of identifying which plant a material comes from; it shows no cannabis and no testing laboratory.

A flowering Andrographis paniculata plant with narrow green leaves and slender seed pods against a dark green background. The article names this herb as the cheaper plant substituted for the bitter tonic Swertia chirata.

Illustrative photo: an ABI 3100 capillary DNA sequencer with its door open, showing the capillary array, syringes and a laser warning label. The four questions the sentence lists could be answered with DNA tools; this is an example of the equipment, not one used in the article.

Illustrative photo: the California State Capitol in Sacramento, a white domed building with a columned portico and a lawn in front. The sentence covers the five states the article examined; California is one of them.
Illustrative photo: an interior stairwell and arches inside the Colorado State Capitol in Denver. The slide names California, Colorado and Michigan; Colorado is one of the three.

Illustrative photo: an Agilent 1200 series liquid chromatography instrument beside a mass spectrometer in a laboratory. A certificate of analysis reports chemical content measured by instruments of this kind; this is not a laboratory named in the article.

Illustrative photo: the west front of the United States Capitol with its dome, seen from the west with the Ulysses S. Grant Memorial in front. Congress passed the hemp provisions the slide describes; this is a general view of the building, not a document or a vote.

Illustrative photo: a researcher in a white coat working at a laboratory bench under a ventilated hood in FDA Life Sciences Laboratory I, Building 64 of the Food and Drug Administration campus in Silver Spring, Maryland. The slide discusses an FDA guidance; this is an agency laboratory, not a document.

Illustrative photo: two blue-and-white painted ceramic pharmacy jars from the Metropolitan Museum of Art collection, each decorated with an animal. The slide quotes a rule about promises made on a container or label; these jars are not the subject of any case in the article.
Illustrative photo: the Illinois State Capitol in Springfield in winter, with its gray dome, seen across a snowy lawn. The fact card lists the rule sets of five states, Illinois among them.

Illustrative photo: the Plant Science Building at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. The article compares shared authentication laboratories to the agricultural extension laboratory system; this is one university plant science building, not a named laboratory.
Illustrative photo: the Michigan State Capitol dome in Lansing, seen against the sky. The know box rests partly on Michigan's testing rules; this is the state's capitol, not a document.
Illustrative photo: the New York State Capitol in Albany, a gray stone building with red roofs and a long facade. The don't box says New York's test menu was not read; this is the state's capitol.

Illustrative photo: a row of closed wooden herbarium cabinets with labeled doors in the Botanical Museum in Helsinki. A herbarium is where reference specimens are kept for checking what a plant is, which is the habit of asking the species question.

posts.title: What one fact check changed
posts.summary: A long piece about a Dutch lake had 134 claims in its map. A second reader, who did not write it, tested every one against the sources themselves. Here is what came back, row by row, from the studio's own files.

The two faces of a darkened silver medal side by side: a standing woman with sheaves of grain beside a sea god in a chariot, and a face covered in lines of Latin capital letters.

onScreen: A second reader checked all 136 claims in one long piece. 113 held. 22 were corrected. 1 was cut.
The draft said RN never saw the old lake bed. Her plane landed on it. Schiphol stands on the drained Haarlemmermeer, about 4 meters below the Dutch zero level.
The draft called Leeghwater a millwright. The source: a carpenter by trade who sometimes called himself a millmaker.
The draft said the museum named no maker. It names two. Engraved by Gerard Coeck after a design by Leeghwater, about 1640 to 1642.
The museum typed SAECVLV. The medal itself reads SAECVLA. When the object and its description disagree, the object wins.
Three checks that day: 16% to 28% of claims needed a fix. A second reader is in the standard for this reason.

posts.title: Effortless for Whom?
posts.summary: When a service becomes easier for one person, the work behind it has to go somewhere. Five sets of public documents, from a Senate committee, a federal safety agency, the Treasury, the Federal Trade Commission and New York City, show where it went and who paid for it.

slides.alt: A paragraph of black report text on white. It says a rate of 600 means workers complete the same tasks every six seconds for a ten-hour shift, 5,400 times per day.
A page of report text under a bold heading about Project Elderwand. The last paragraph gives an upper limit of 1,940 repetitions in a ten-hour shift, about 216 items per hour.
A two-column table of Amazon warehouse injury rates per year: 7.25 in 2017, 7.74 in 2018, 9.01 in 2019, 6.59 in 2020, 7.64 in 2021, 6.97 in 2022 and 6.54 in 2023.
A scanned legal page headed Resolution and Amendment of Citation Items. A one-row table for site MDW8 shows an original penalty of $15,625 and an amended penalty of $145,000.
A table titled Direct File Costs per Filing Season. Tax year 2023: 140,803 filers, $31.8 million, $225.85 per return. Tax year 2024: 296,531 filers, $41 million, $138.27 per return.

The top of a court filing with a blue header line giving the case number, Document 490 and page 10 of 47. Numbered lines say that once a Prime member enters Iliad, they must reaffirm their desire to cancel on three pages.

A court order page with numbered lines and a blue header for Document 535. It requires cancellation through the same medium used to consent and a clear button to decline, which cannot say no thanks, I don't want free shipping.

sources.label: Senate HELP majority staff report (Dec 2024)

onScreen: One envelope every six seconds, 5,400 times a day. A Senate staff report did the math from what Amazon workers said.
An Amazon study set a limit: 1,940 picks a shift. Staff say Amazon rejected it. Amazon says the break pilot did not work.
One set of numbers, two readings. Amazon's rate fell from 9.01 in 2019 to 6.54 in 2023. In 2017 it was 7.25.
OSHA and Amazon settled ten cases in December 2024. One citation was kept and raised to $145,000, with no admission.
The IRS carried the work, then counted the bill. At least $138.27 a return in the 2025 season. Treasury suspended it.
To cancel Prime, members confirmed on three pages. A federal judge described Amazon's cancel flow, which it called Iliad.
The 2025 settlement: cancel the way you signed up. $2.5 billion. And the decline button cannot say no to free shipping.

posts.title: Who Sees Your Cannabis File
posts.summary: A dispensary may sit outside HIPAA. A door check, a state tracking system, a registry, police lookups and a provider's files each follow their own rules.

slides.alt: Part of page 5 of OMCCR's September 2024 newsletter. It says that while a medical cannabis dispensary may not be subject to HIPAA laws, Hawaiʻi Administrative Rules section 11-850-40 requires every dispensary to safeguard and keep confidential any personally identifying information and the medical condition of a patient.

Part of a page of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-850, section 11-850-33. A retail dispensing location must require a government-issued photo identification and a registration card before entry and must log the name and entry and exit time of every person who enters.

Part of 45 CFR 160.103 in the 2025 Code of Federal Regulations. It defines a covered entity as a health plan, a health care clearinghouse, or a health care provider who transmits health information electronically in connection with a covered transaction.

The text of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329-131, as printed from the saved web page. It says the prescription requirements of section 329-38 and the board of pharmacy licensure rules do not apply to the medical use of cannabis.

Page 850-48 of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-850, section 11-850-40, Confidentiality of information. It says a dispensary licensee shall safeguard and keep confidential any personally identifying information and the medical condition of a qualifying patient.

Part of page 5 of OMCCR's September 2024 newsletter. It says OMCCR does not share a patient's qualifying conditions with dispensaries, and that the 329 card registration number, name and date of birth are verified at a dispensary.

Part of page 850-60 of the dispensary rules, section 11-850-61(b) and (c). A dispensary shall track electronically all sales to patients from all dispensaries in the State and have a sales system that blocks sales over the legal limits and cannot be overridden manually.

The start of Hawaii Administrative Rules section 11-160-56, Confidential information; exceptions. It says information the department keeps to administer the chapter is confidential except to employees and agents of the department, law enforcement, people with a court order, and others on a list.
The text of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329D-20, Law enforcement access to dispensary and production center records, as printed from the saved web page.

The definition of personal information in Hawaii Revised Statutes section 487N-1, as printed from the saved web page: a name combined with a Social Security number, a driver's license or Hawaii identification card number, or a financial account number with an access code.

A column of page 22715 of the Federal Register of April 28, 2026, in the Drug Enforcement Administration final rule that places FDA-approved products and marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license in schedule III and sets up an expedited registration process.

Part of the CMS web page Are You a Covered Entity, as printed from the saved copy. It says providers who submit HIPAA transactions, like claims, electronically are covered, and lists doctors, clinics, dentists and pharmacies as examples.
slides.credit: Source: CMS, covered entities page, PD

slides.alt: The start of section 11-850-151, Remedies, in the dispensary rules. It says the director may serve a notice of violation and an order that can require a violator to stop, pay an administrative penalty and submit a corrective action plan.

posts.title: Snap and send: eight photo stops in the Netherlands
posts.summary: A station, a lamp factory, a flying saucer, a design festival, an AI expo and a national museum: what each place is, what the rules let a visitor post the same day, and what the camera roll from the trip shows.

posts.title: The Golf Balls Above Kaʻena Point Tracked America’s Early Satellite Programs
posts.summary: In 1959 the Air Force opened a tracking station on the ridge above Oʻahu's western tip. Its first job was a secret: helping bring film home from America's first photo satellites. The declassified histories, the newspapers of 1960 and the federal surveys of its buildings show what the station did, how it worked and how it changed.

slides.alt: A single white radome sits on a green ridge above the blue Pacific at Kaʻena Point Space Force Station, photographed in September 2022. It is the actual golf ball of the title, shown as it looks today, not in the CORONA era.
slides.credit: Photo: Brooke Wise, USSF, Public domain

slides.alt: A large white radome and a smaller one beside a dish antenna stand on a grassy ridge above the ocean at the Kaʻena Point Satellite Tracking Station, photographed in 2008. It shows the radomes the opening sentence describes.

Typed page 10 of the federal survey of the Kaʻena Point station, HAER HI-97. It lists the land's owners from the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi to the State and the Campbell Estate, with the Army and then the Air Force as lessees from 1958, and says the original site was land leased from the Territory of Hawaiʻi and private owners, 106 acres in 1958.

Typed Significance section of the federal survey, HAER HI-97 page 7. It says the station was established in 1958 to support the CORONA/Discoverer Satellite Program, that the nation's first satellite reconnaissance program was named Discoverer and became known by its codeword CORONA, and that the station, then known as HULA, supported it with data retrieval, tracking and relay.

The camera system built for the Discoverer and CORONA satellites on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 2012: a long metal frame holding the camera and film machinery, with the gold capsule that brought the film back to Earth at its right end. It is the system that first returned photographs from orbit.

The CIA's line drawing titled Satellite Control Facility Operation in Recovery: three dashed satellite passes over Alaska, ENABLE commands from the control center and Vandenberg (STC, VTS) and a backup from Kodiak (KTS), Control arrows from the control center to the stations, and the Hawaii Tracking Station (HTS) at the bottom sending Control to a recovery plane near the capsule's impact point.
slides.credit: Source: CIA CORONA history, vol. 4, PD

slides.alt: Typed lines from page 229 of the NRO's declassification guide, section 5, Operations: MGS and RTS. Under Redact, item a reads: Redact specific details about the Mission Ground Station or Remote Tracking Station commands that were uplinked to the satellite, i.e., orbit adjustment, deorbit, camera operations, SIGINT payload operations, etc.
slides.credit: Source: NRO redaction guide, p. 229, PD

slides.alt: Typed list from page 52 of the NRO's declassification guide: Release fact that the following remote tracking stations supported DISCOVERER (CORONA) and/or SAMOS reconnaissance satellite programs, followed by ten sites from Annette Island, Alaska, to Vandenberg AFB, California, with Kaena Point, Hawaii, fourth.
slides.credit: Source: NRO redaction guide, p. 52, PD

slides.alt: Photograph of a CORONA parachute bag from the CIA Museum: an olive-green nylon pack with webbing straps and laced seams. It held the parachute that opened after the film capsule separated from the spacecraft and slowed it on the way down.
A black-and-white U.S. Air Force photograph of a C-119J Flying Boxcar towing a CORONA film capsule on its parachute after a midair catch. The photo is not identified as a Hawaiʻi recovery.
slides.credit: Source: U.S. Air Force, Public domain

slides.alt: Close view of the nose, cockpit windows and left propeller of the C-119J Flying Boxcar marked 037, now at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force. It is the Hickam-based plane, Pelican 9, whose crew caught the Discoverer XIV film capsule in midair in August 1960.

A CORONA recovery vehicle, the gold-colored capsule shell that carried exposed film back through re-entry, on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in 2008. It is one of the very different machines in the chain of custody.
A CORONA film canister with its lid off and a spool of film beside it, photographed by the CIA. It is the physical object that had to move from the recovered capsule to secure processing elsewhere.

The CIA's chart titled CORONA Program Synopsis: a curve of total launches rising from 1959 to 1972, labels for program firsts from First Polar Orbit and First Air Recovery to Last CORONA Series Flight, and a table at the bottom: 8 launches and no recoveries in 1959, 11 launches and 4 recoveries in 1960, and the program running to 1972. Two blank white boxes are the CIA's redactions.
slides.credit: Source: CIA CORONA history, vol. 1, PD

slides.alt: A brass CORONA retrieval hook wrapped in tape and rope, on display at the Smithsonian's Udvar-Hazy Center in Virginia in 2018. Eight hooks like it hung from a frame behind the recovery plane and snagged the capsule's parachute, the recovery step at the end of the list.

Looking along the Waiʻanae coast from above Keawaʻula Bay: a sunlit slope in the foreground, the bay and cliffs to the right, and the station radomes small on the ridge at the far left, photographed in September 2022. It shows how the station sits inside a wider landscape.
slides.credit: Photo: Brooke Wise, USSF, Public domain

slides.alt: The entrance to Kaʻena Point Space Force Station on 17 June 2021, with the new Space Force sign beside the road and the Waiʻanae mountains behind. It was taken the month the station was renamed.

An aerial view of the Kaʻena Point station released for its 55th anniversary: two white radomes on the ridge, the road, a helipad and the operations building above the ocean. It shows the two sides of the station the sentence describes.
slides.credit: Photo: Jason Gabrick, USAF, Public domain

onScreen: The Golf Balls Above Kaʻena Point Tracked America’s Early Satellite Programs
From the Waiʻanae coast, the white radomes above Kaʻena Point look almost abstract: two geometric objects placed against a ridge.
In 1958, the United States Air Force began building what was then known as the HULA tracking station on land leased from the Territory of Hawaiʻi and private landowners.
Operations began in February 1959. Its initial mission supported Discoverer, the public-facing name associated with the classified CORONA reconnaissance-satellite program.
CORONA was the first American satellite program to return photographs from orbit.
Commands could concern orbit adjustments, camera operations and deorbit sequences.
CORONA exposed physical film in space. A reentry capsule separated from the spacecraft, descended toward Earth and deployed a parachute.
Recovery aircraft attempted to catch it in midair; ships could retrieve capsules that reached the ocean.
An official Air Force history of Kaʻena says aircraft from Hickam and ships from Pearl Harbor participated in recovery.
The capsule then had to move into secure processing and interpretation elsewhere. Kaʻena did not develop the film or interpret the photographs.
The first fully successful CORONA mission occurred in August 1960, after a string of failures that demonstrated how many systems had to work at once:
The station’s mission outlived CORONA. It became part of the Air Force Satellite Control Network and, in 2021, was renamed Kaʻena Point Space Force Station.
Read the declassified documents Read the land and place limitations Read the image rights Read the full story at Tech From Here: Hawaiʻi

onScreen: McDonald's Canada ran the same promotional idea twice under two different official names: International Menu Heist in 2025, then World Menu Heist in 2026.
In June 2025, McDonald's Canada's International Menu Heist brought six items to Canada for a limited time, including Japan's Teriyaki Chicken Sandwich and Germany's Big Rösti burger.
The idea cast each item as a flavor taken in a “heist” from another country's McDonald's menu, Italy's McPizza Bites and Belgium's Biscoff McFlurry were also part of the 2025 lineup.
In August 2026, McDonald's Canada brought the idea back as World Menu Heist, with a new seven-item lineup including Australia's Chicken Parmi Burger and Spain's McExtreme Pulled Pork.
The 2025 and 2026 menus did not share a single item, 2025: International Menu Heist, June 2025, six items 2026: World Menu Heist, August 2026, seven items
Japan's Teriyaki Chicken Sandwich never appeared alongside Australia's Chicken Parmi Burger. Items shared: None
Each year's campaign needs its own menu list, its own launch date and its own citation, 2025's International Menu Heist and 2026's World Menu Heist should never be cited as one continuous menu.
What we know: McDonald’s Canada ran two campaigns, International Menu Heist in 2025 and World Menu Heist in 2026.
What we don't: It does not establish continuity of every product, market or right.

posts.title: After Hilo Had No Warning, Hawaiʻi Helped Build a Pacific One
posts.summary: On April 1, 1946, a wave from the Aleutian Islands reached Hilo almost five hours after it formed, and no one told the town it was coming. The reports, tide gauges and survivor accounts show what Hawaiʻi built next, and what a warning still cannot do on its own.

slides.alt: Aerial photograph of downtown Hilo and Hilo Bay on 1 April 1946, taken from the air after the tsunami: rows of commercial blocks sit behind a shoreline strip scattered with wreckage, with a ship lying offshore. The mount is captioned “Tidal Wave Damage, Hilo, Hawaii, T.H. (1 Apr. 1946).” It opens the story on the town the tsunami reached with no warning.
slides.credit: Photo: U.S. Army Air Forces (NARA), PD
slides.url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hawaii_-_Hilo_-_NARA_-_23937271.jpg (NARA catalog https://catalog.archives.gov/id/23937271, RG 18 Airscapes series, local id 18-AA-37-15)

slides.alt: Photograph of a Hilo street after the 1 April 1946 tsunami: splintered timber from smashed buildings fills the roadway, a car is half buried in the debris, and storefront signs for Cafe 100 and Hilo Products still hang along the covered sidewalk. It shows the damage behind the Hilo figures, not the people counted.
slides.credit: Source: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Obs., PD

slides.alt: Photograph of the white stone memorial at Laupāhoehoe Point, Hawaiʻi Island, engraved “In memory of those who lost their lives in the tidal wave, April 1, 1946,” with a list of names and ages and fresh flower leis, fruit and shells laid at its base. It marks the Laupāhoehoe school community the sentence names.

Color photograph, circa 1960, of the Coast and Geodetic Survey Honolulu Observatory at Ewa Beach on Oʻahu: a brick sign reading United States Department of Commerce, Coast and Geodetic Survey, Honolulu Observatory, Geomagnetism, Seismology, with low observatory buildings, a flagpole and a car behind. It shows the observatory that housed the warning operation; the Ewa site dates from about 1960, after the 1948 start.

onScreen: After Hilo Had No Warning, Hawaiʻi Helped Build a Pacific One The earthquake had occurred thousands of miles away in the Aleutian Islands.
The 1946 tsunami killed 96 people in Hilo, and NOAA’s tsunami database lists $26 million in damage across Hawaiʻi (in 1946 dollars).
Waves struck elsewhere in the Hawaiian Islands, and Laupāhoehoe’s school community carries its own devastating history.
In 1948, the United States established its first tsunami warning operation at the Honolulu Magnetic and Seismic Observatory.
NOAA’s tsunami.gov history dates official U.S. tsunami warning capability to 1949. The system as the Coast and Geodetic Survey drew it in 1950.
The facts, in numbers
Tide gauges could confirm abnormal sea-level movement. The Kahului, Maui, gauge as the 1957 tsunami arrived.
Museums, survivor accounts, school lessons, memorials and repeated drills preserve information the live sensor network cannot supply: what a confusing morning felt like, which cues people noticed,
why some instructions were trusted, where movement became impossible and how the coastline changed afterward.
In 1946, the Pacific had enough distance to permit a warning, but no institution capable of producing one.

onScreen: Who gets to decide what gets seen?
The festival's own organizer asked for this dinner. SHOW NOT SHOW hosted the official DDW opening dinner for the international press at the Dutch Design Foundation's request.
The title borrows from Jacqueline Hassink. In 1993 to 1995 she asked Europe's 40 largest industrial firms to photograph their boardroom tables. 19 refused; each got a black photo.
The furniture was part of the show. Frank Penders and Luuk van Laarhoven made the table. Dear Objects' new BARRICADA stools and benches were used at the dinner.
One magazine reported from inside the dinner. Guests were invited to get up and share the power, Dezeen reported. It saw few journalists do so.
Reporters reach the festival through a form. DDW's press form asks for links to your recent coverage and the subjects you plan to cover.
What the documents show
Visibility comes from ordinary choices.

posts.title: c14-01 Steel guitar (Tech From Here, second run; its filmed Reel is the registry's c14-01 A; Hawaiian-language and cultural check before posting)
posts.summary: A boy from Lāʻie, a bar of polished steel and a new way to play the guitar. Old newspapers, discs, a patent and a Hawaiʻi law show how the sound left Oʻahu and how its name got lost along the way.

slides.alt: A handmade steel guitar in a Country Music Hall of Fame display case, shown with its museum label and a Milton Brown and His Musical Brownies poster. It opens the story because it puts a steel guitar inside country music, the place most listeners hear it.

A grainy 1912 newspaper halftone of Joseph Kekuku, seated in a pale suit and dark lei, both hands resting on an instrument laid flat across his lap, inside a printed frame. The Los Angeles Times printed it while he toured the mainland. It sits on the boundary slide because Kekuku is the name tied to the instrument, while the later accounts leave the first moment unrecoverable.

A halftone newspaper photograph of five men in matching white tunics with dark sashes, holding ukuleles and guitars, printed on page 6 of The Colville Examiner of July 22, 1916 under a headline about Hawaiian music at the Chautauqua; the article text names Kekuku's Hawaiian quintette. Cropped to the photograph from a full-resolution page image. It follows the boundary slide because the working life of a touring musician, not a single discovery, is where the story picks up.

Hawaiian steel guitarist Bobby Ingano seated on a folding chair on a cemetery lawn in Kāneʻohe, Oʻahu, in January 2024, a lap steel guitar flat across his knees and a small amplifier beside him, playing at the grave of the musician Gabby Pahinui. It shows a Hawaiian musician still performing the technique the slide names.
slides.credit: Photo: Michael Kiese / Puʻuloa Hawaiian Band, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.alt: Page 6 of The Original Guckert's Chords for the Hawaiian Steel Guitar, 1917: three chord grids for the key of C and, below, drawings of the steel bar held straight across the strings for C and slanted for F and G. It is an instruction book turning the technique into diagrams, the exact thing the slide says.
slides.credit: Page: Guckert, Union Music Co., 1917, PD, cropped

slides.alt: A Rickenbacker Electro B6 lap steel guitar from the late 1930s lying on a grey surface, photographed from above, with its chrome-covered horseshoe-magnet pickup set under the strings near the bridge. Commons describes it as having the Beauchamp horseshoe pickup. It shows the part the sentence names: the pickup that turns the vibration of the metal strings into an electrical signal for an amplifier.

A 1934 aluminum-cast Ro-Pat-In 'Frying Pan' electric lap steel guitar in a museum case at the Museum of Making Music. It is the instrument form the sentence describes, the lap steel tied to Beauchamp, Rickenbacker and the Ro-Pat-In company.

The 1931 one-piece maple prototype of the Rickenbacker Frying Pan electric lap steel guitar, a round solid body with a long neck and a pickup under the strings, standing in a glass display case with reflections and a museum label behind it. Commons credits its design to George Beauchamp, Paul Barth and Harry Watson. It is the kind of instrument the patent describes, an electrical stringed instrument with no conventional soundboard or resonance box. It is a photograph of the object, not of the patent.

Sheet 1 of the drawings for U.S. Patent 2,089,171, headed Aug. 10, 1937, G. D. Beauchamp, Electrical Stringed Musical Instrument, Filed June 2, 1934: the round solid body and long neck from the front, and the horseshoe magnet pickup under the strings. It is the patent's own drawing of an instrument with no sound hole or soundboard.

A 1938 Farm Security Administration photograph of a guitarist playing a steel-bodied guitar at a microphone during a Cajun band contest at the National Rice Festival in Crowley, Louisiana. It shows the technique far from Hawaiʻi, already part of another community's music.
slides.credit: Photo: Russell Lee, FSA, public domain

slides.alt: A photograph of the center label of a Victor 78 rpm disc, number 18569-B, Tomi Tomi (Hawaiian Hula Hula), credited to the Hawaiian Quintette with Hawaiian stringed instruments and drawn from the incidental music to Richard Walton Tully's play The Bird of Paradise; the Hawaiʻi State Archives dates the performance April 11, 1913. The label names the song, the group, the playwright and the company, and none of the players. It carries the questions about who is credited and who is remembered.
slides.credit: Label: Victor, 1913, PD; HI State Archives

slides.alt: A two-neck electric console steel guitar on four steel legs, built in Detroit between 1961 and 1963 by Felton W. Williams Jr., a steel player in the House of God church, now at the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. It closes the story because it is the same technology in a gospel tradition, one of the traditions the final sentence names.

posts.title: Why Human Review Requires Authority, Context and Time
posts.summary: Three public investigations looked at people placed beside automated systems: a test driver in Arizona, compliance officers in Australia and airline pilots over Indonesia and Ethiopia. Their reports show what each person could change, what each could see, and how many seconds or cases they were given.

slides.alt: The top of an NTSB table with columns for time to impact, speed, classification and path prediction, and system actions. At 5.6 seconds radar makes first detection of the pedestrian, classified as a vehicle; at 5.2 seconds lidar detects an unknown object.

Two rows of the NTSB table. At 1.2 seconds the bicycle is fully on the SUV's path, steering around it is no longer possible, and action suppression begins. At 0.2 seconds action suppression ends, and an auditory alert sounds.
A paragraph of NTSB report text saying that about five months before the crash the company began testing with one operator, removing a layer of safety redundancy and adding tasks for that operator.

A paragraph of report text: where compliance officers had been involved, the entire process would now be conducted online, the aim being to reduce (and preferably obviate) human involvement at the DHS end.

A red heading, 3.1 Staff concerns, above three paragraphs of report text. The last says that from around September 2015 compliance officers would no longer contact employers, and from January 2016 would no longer check a recipient's departmental file.
A paragraph of NTSB report text followed by four bullet points listing Boeing's assumptions, including that unexpected inputs are readily recognizable and that the pilot will take immediate action.

Three short paragraphs of guidance text. The middle one says oversight of a decision must be meaningful, rather than a token gesture, and carried out by someone with the authority and competence to change the decision.

For one second, the system held back its own braking. No alert told the driver the pause had begun. Uber called it action suppression.
About five months earlier, Uber cut the second operator. The NTSB: that removed a layer of safety redundancy.
Robodebt aimed to reduce human involvement. And preferably to make it unnecessary, a Royal Commission found.
Officers stopped calling employers, then checking files. From September 2015 and January 2016.

posts.title: Two strikes at once: where 'intersectionality' came from
posts.summary: The word began in a 1989 law review article about court cases. This is the story of those cases: five women laid off from a car plant, the judge who said their claim could not be "a combination of both," the courts that disagreed, and a hiring dispute at a law school in Honolulu.

onScreen: IKEA’s BILLY bookcase instructions can guide a complete stranger from flat-pack parts to a finished bookcase without a single meeting.
They begin by showing the parts and tools before assembly starts.
Then each step arrives in a sequence the builder can follow.
Checks along the way prevent one early mistake from becoming the final result.
The finished state is visible: Inputs: Parts and tools shown first Sequence: Each step in an order the builder can follow
the bookcase stands, aligns and works. Checks: Catch one early mistake before it becomes the result Finished state: Visible: the bookcase stands, aligns and works
A creator brief works the same way: it’s the operating system that turns inputs, sequence and checks into a finished result anyone can build.
“Make it feel premium” hides a room full of unanswered decisions. What we know: A vague instruction like “Make it feel premium” leaves many decisions unanswered.
What we don't know: The example does not establish that the language is common or intentionally misleading.

posts.title: A Right You Cannot Use
posts.summary: A check stopped before a hearing. A man crawled up courthouse stairs. A judge left one line on a form blank. Four Supreme Court cases show what turns a right on paper into a right a person can use.

slides.alt: Two columns of printed court opinion text side by side. The left says Angela Velez was cut off on March 11, 1968, because her husband allegedly visited every night, and that the tip came from her landlady and was untrue. The right says she and her four children were evicted before the decision.
slides.credit: Source: Kelly v. Wyman, 294 F. Supp. 893

slides.alt: A page of a 1970 Supreme Court opinion, headed 264, October Term, 1969, with a paragraph saying ending aid during a dispute may deprive an eligible person of the very means by which to live while he waits.
Opinion text across two pages, joined by a thin gray line, saying the delay between a hearing request and a decision is between 10 and 11 months and the full delay exceeds one year.

Printed federal regulation text headed section 404.1597a, in two stacked pieces, saying a person who wants benefits to continue must request reconsideration and continuation of benefits no later than 10 days after receiving the notice.

Opinion text across two pages, joined by a thin gray line, saying Lane was ordered to a second-floor courtroom with no elevator, crawled up two flights of stairs at his first appearance, and was later jailed for failure to appear.

Printed opinion text: the judge filled out a form titled Order for Contempt of Court with the line Defendant (was) (was not) gainfully employed and/or (had) (did not have) the ability to make these support payments when due, and left the statement as is.

Two columns of printed rule text side by side. The left begins section 303.6, Enforcement of support obligations, (c)(4) Establishing guidelines for the use of civil contempt citations. The right lists (i) screen the case for ability to pay, (ii) provide the court with that information, and (iii) provide clear notice that ability to pay constitutes the critical question.

Bar chart with four bars on a scale of 0 to 100 percent: 25 percent of serious problems got a search for legal help, 92 percent got no or not enough help, 46 percent of non-seekers named cost, and 49 percent of legal aid requests were turned away.

onScreen: New York cut off Angela Velez's welfare in 1968. The tip was false. Her family was evicted before she won.
In 1970 the Supreme Court said: hold the hearing first. A cutoff can take the means to live while a person waits.
By 1976, disability appeals took more than a year. The Court still did not require a hearing before the cutoff.
Since 1983, benefits can continue during an appeal. Ask within 10 days of the notice, Social Security's rule says.
George Lane crawled up two flights of stairs to reach court. The courthouse had no elevator. In 2004 the Court let his ADA suit go on.
The judge left the ability-to-pay line blank. He got 12 months in jail. The Supreme Court said that broke due process.
Since 2016, a federal rule requires a clear notice. Child support agencies must tell a parent that ability to pay is the critical question.
Too little or no legal help for 92% of serious problems. Low-income Americans, in a 2022 Legal Services Corporation study.

posts.title: Vonnegut's shapes of stories, and what the data found
posts.summary: He drew the curves on a blackboard, then used Hamlet to show where they fail. The studies that tested his idea found that the arcs readers chose most often did not simply end high.

onScreen: Vonnegut drew the shapes of stories, then tested them on Hamlet.
Cinderella: up in steps, down at midnight, up again. As Vonnegut drew it in A Man Without a Country (2005).
Kafka's man wakes up as a cockroach. His line drops off the scale.
Hamlet's ghost: good news or bad? Vonnegut said no one can tell. He called that the truth, and the reason the play is great.
2016: a computer scored 1,327 books, 10,000 words at a time. Six shapes came back.
Most downloaded: not the happy rise. Medians: doubled Man in a Hole 105.5, Icarus 97, rise 80, single hole 76.
Films: Man in a Hole led the box office. Mean domestic gross, 6,174 films: $37.48 million.
Change the measure, change the winner. Decide what success means first.

posts.title: Between Lights
posts.summary: Teresa van Dongen's Between Lights put solar harvesting where people look. The published numbers on see-through solar cells show what that costs, and what the public documents leave open.

slides.alt: The designer's visualization of Between Lights: a three-pane window looking out over a lake and hills, with a band of blue square modules patterned with yellow diamonds running across all three panes, above a window seat with cushions and candles. It is a visualization from the press kit, not a photograph of the installation. Slide text: A window that makes power by day and light by night. Teresa van Dongen's Between Lights, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, as she pictured it.
slides.credit: Image: Teresa van Dongen, DDW press kit

slides.alt: A gloved hand holding a small square organic solar cell of the polymer-blend kind, a reddish, partly see-through glass slide with rows of round silver contacts. It is a lab-scale cell of the kind the festival text names; it is not Between Lights. Slide text: Its panels used organic solar cells, which can be printed thin. They collected sunlight and indoor light, the festival text said.

Bar chart of two see-through lab solar cells. The color-neutral cell let 43.3 percent of visible light through and turned 8.1 percent of sunlight into power; the green-tinted cell 45.7 and 10.8 percent. Slide text: A see-through solar cell trades view for power. In a 2020 lab test, one cell let 43 percent of visible light through and turned 8 percent of sunlight into power.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from PNAS 2020 data

slides.alt: Bar chart of yearly output in a Dutch test: a south panel tilted at about 35 degrees is 100, an upright south-facing panel about 70, and an upright panel turned 60 degrees east or west about 65. Slide text: A window also faces the sun at a poor angle. In a Dutch test, upright south-facing panels made about 70 percent of a tilted panel's yearly power.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Hanze 2019 data

slides.alt: A microscope view of the pointed tip of a Canadian pondweed leaf, its cells packed with green chloroplasts along a central vein, against a black background. Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens; it is not Between Lights. Slide text: The designer named photosynthesis as her inspiration. Over a year, plants turn about 1 to 2 percent of sunlight into biomass, a U.S. energy lab said in 2011.

Bar chart of typical indoor light levels from a 2021 review: homes about 200 lux, offices about 500 lux and workshops about 1,500 lux; sunlight is about 1,000 times stronger. Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: The panels collected sunlight and indoor light, and lit LEDs at dusk. What we don't: How much power that made, how much was stored, how long the LEDs ran.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from ChemSusChem data

slides.alt: The Klokgebouw at Strijp-S in Eindhoven under a blue sky: a white former Philips factory block with a clock tower. It is the building where Between Lights was shown.
