posts.title: Can the Institution Be Answered?
posts.summary: A computer called workers cheats and no person checked. Teachers could not test their own scores. An agency left airbags out of its reasons. A cabinet memo gave a reason the Supreme Court found contrived. Four disputes show what it takes to answer an institution, and to make it answer back.

slides.alt: A page of a 2019 federal appeals court opinion with two paragraphs: from October 2013 to August 2015 the system alone decided fraud and no human being took part, and the questionnaires went to online accounts, many of them dormant.
slides.credit: Source: Cahoo v. SAS Analytics (6th Cir.)

slides.alt: Printed court opinion text quoting a questionnaire: a yes or no question about giving false information, then eight numbered reasons starting with I needed the money, and a sentence saying the form gave no information about why the agency suspected fraud.
slides.credit: Source: Cahoo v. SAS Analytics (6th Cir.)

slides.alt: Bar chart with three bars on a 0 to 100 percent scale: 85 percent of fraud findings made by the computer alone reversed, 44 percent of findings sent to staff reversed, and, for comparison, 41 percent of all appeals reversed or changed by judges.
slides.credit: Chart: RN Collins, from Michigan UIA data

slides.alt: Two pieces of a printed state law joined by a thin gray line: the heading Act No. 226, Public Acts of 2017, approved by the Governor December 20, 2017, then subsection (m) saying the agency shall not make a determination based solely on a computer-identified discrepancy, and enacting sections giving July 1, 2018.

Scanned court opinion text across two pages, joined by a thin gray line, saying trade secrets do not let a school district violate its employees' rights, and that the proper remedy is to overturn the policy while leaving the trade secrets intact.
slides.credit: Source: HFT v. Houston ISD (S.D. Tex.)

slides.alt: Two pieces of a 1983 Supreme Court page, 48, October Term 1982, joined by a thin gray line: the heading, then lines saying the agency did not even consider requiring airbags in its 1981 rulemaking and that not one sentence of its statement discusses the airbags-only option.

onScreen: Michigan's computer decided unemployment fraud with no person involved. That is what people suing said of 2013 to 2015, and a federal court took it as true.
Flagged workers got two questions and ten days to answer. The form never said why the agency suspected them.
When the agency rechecked in 2017, it reversed 85% of computer-only fraud findings. Where an investigator took part, it reversed 44%.
Michigan's law bars fraud findings based only on a computer mismatch. An agency employee must examine the facts first. This version applied from July 2018.
Houston rated teachers with scores no teacher could check. In 2017 a federal judge said the remedy was to overturn the policy and leave the trade secrets intact.
In 1983 the Supreme Court found a safety agency never considered requiring airbags. "Not one sentence of its rulemaking statement discusses the airbags-only option."
In 2019 the Court said the census question's stated reason "seems to have been contrived." It sent the decision back to the agency.
A 2023 federal framework lists ways for people to appeal what an AI system decides. NIST calls the framework voluntary.

posts.title: License or buyout?
posts.summary: In 1984 a film producer ordered special effects shots, and no one said a word about who would own them. The court case that followed, and four others like it, show what a payment buys, what it leaves behind, and why the answer belongs on paper before the work travels.

What answers it: The contract, not the invoice or upload, must answer what moved Then define: Media, term, territory, edits, paid use and sublicensing
Vague language can still be misunderstood, or stretched in practice.
Creator and brand need the same answer about what the brand may use. What we know: If ownership is not transferred, the deal is usually a license.

For an Institution of One, scope protects price, control and future work.
Write media, term, territory, edits, paid use and sublicensing.
Name the deal. Define the use. Keep the boundary visible.

posts.title: Why Evidence Systems, Not Model Intelligence, Are the Missing Layer
posts.summary: Courts in New York and London have now ruled on filings built from answers that no one checked, and Parliament had to undo hundreds of convictions that rested on a computer's word. The court papers show where each evidence path broke, who was supposed to catch it, and what it took to repair the damage.

The prompts: “provide case law,” “show me more cases.” The chatbot complied by making them up, the court found.
The lawyer who signed read it for flow and grammar. He checked none of the cases it cited, the court found.
A London court counted 45 citations in one case. In 18, the case cited does not exist.
Check AI research against authoritative sources. England's High Court named those sources in June 2025.
In the Post Office cases, the computer was the only evidence. “There was no evidence of a shortfall other than the Horizon data.”
A 2024 law quashed the convictions. 620 people. 584 told by letter by September 2026.

posts.title: Beyond Personal Software: Your AI Is Becoming a Private Institution
posts.summary: A judge in New York ordered OpenAI to keep chats its users had deleted. European law lets people take their data with them, but official guidance leaves out what a system inferred about them. Read in order, the court orders, laws and regulator files show what a person can ask of a system that acts for them, and where those rights end.

slides.alt: A typed court paragraph directing OpenAI to preserve and segregate all output log data that would otherwise be deleted, then So Ordered, dated May 13, 2025, with the judge's e-signature.

Typed court text with two numbered paragraphs: one ends the obligation to preserve deleted output logs as of September 26, 2025; the other keeps logs already preserved, except those from the European Economic Area, Switzerland or the United Kingdom.

A paragraph of court text on the order to produce the entire de-identified 20 million log sample, listing three privacy protections: a smaller sample, de-identification and the existing protective order.
Two paragraphs of guidance text saying inferred and derived data, such as a health assessment or a credit score, are created by the controller and fall outside the right to data portability.
Printed legal text headed Automated individual decision-making, including profiling, ending with the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision.

onScreen: In May 2025, a judge ordered OpenAI to keep chats its users had deleted. A delete button is a promise. A court can override it.
The order ended for new chats on Sept. 26, 2025. Chats already kept stayed kept, except those from the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK.
Then a court ordered 20 million kept chats handed over. Personal details removed first, and a protective order limits who sees them.
EU law lets you take the data you provided. Official guidance says what a system inferred about you does not travel with you.
A recourse template already exists: a human to step in, a chance to be heard and a way to contest an automated decision.
The FTC asked seven chatbot companies in 2025: Do you draw inferences from users' chats? How long do you keep data after a deletion request?
Italy fined OpenAI 15 million euros in 2024. In March 2026, a Rome court annulled the fine: the wrong regulator had issued it.

posts.title: Tiers, Targets, and the Guidance Gap
posts.summary: Multi-target pharmacology appears to be something close to the default operating mode of plant-derived bioactive compounds. The article adds that "default" may overstate how uniform the underlying biology actually is. A close view of tea plant leaves.

Illustrative photo: tea shoots showing two leaves and a bud on a tea plant in Assam, India. One of the three ingredients in the 2019 study, EGCG, is a compound found in tea; the study did not photograph or sample this plant.

posts.title: Luxury Agents: The Next Status Symbol Is Protected Attention
posts.summary: A New York hotel put a telephone in every room in 1904 and later sold a butler to answer for the guest. Software agents now promise the same kind of help online. Read in order, the court orders, rules and regulator files show what the law already asks of anything that guards a person's attention, and what it asks when that person wants to leave.

slides.alt: Two narrow columns of rule text headed Simple cancellation, Click to Cancel, saying the way to cancel must be at least as easy to use as the way the consumer consented.

onScreen: Leaving Amazon Prime took six clicks and fifteen options, the FTC charged. Joining took one or two clicks.
A 2025 court order binds Amazon for ten years: cancelling must not be difficult, costly, confusing or time consuming.
In 2024, the FTC wrote the same idea into a rule for every seller: leaving must be at least as easy as signing up.
In July 2025, an appeals court struck the rule down. It faulted the process the FTC used, not the goal.
EU law bars online platforms from deceptive design. It names leaving that is harder than joining as one practice the Commission may address.
California counted Honda's clicks: one to accept cookies, at least two to opt out. Honda agreed to pay $632,500 and add a Reject All button.
California already has a rule for agents that act for a person: keep the data safe, and use it only for the task.

posts.title: Inhaled Residue
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi tests dispensary cannabis against a list of 56 pesticides, each at one limit. Food runs on a different rulebook. Here is how the two systems work, how other states set their numbers, and where the public sources stop.

slides.alt: Part of page 850-110 of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules section 11-850-135. It lists heavy metal limits in Table 3 and then says pesticides listed in Table 4 each have a limit of 1.0 parts per million.

The start of 21 U.S.C. section 346a in the 2024 United States Code. Paragraph (a)(1) says a pesticide chemical residue in or on a food shall be deemed unsafe unless a tolerance is in effect and the residue is within its limits, or an exemption from the tolerance requirement is in effect.

Part of EPA's Regulation of Pesticide Residues on Food web page, printed from the saved copy. It says EPA sets tolerances, which are the maximum amount of a pesticide allowed to remain in or on a food.

Part of 21 U.S.C. section 346a in the 2024 United States Code, the determination of safety. Safe means a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure, including all anticipated dietary exposures and all other exposures for which there is reliable information.

Part of an EPA slide, Cannabis Status Update, from the November 1, 2017 Pesticide Program Dialogue Committee meeting. It says there are no pesticides registered by EPA specifically for use on marijuana and no tolerances established for marijuana or hemp.
Part of 7 U.S.C. section 136j in the 2024 United States Code. Item (G) makes it unlawful to use any registered pesticide in a manner inconsistent with its labeling.

The top of the Hawaii Department of Agriculture Pesticides Branch document, Criteria for Pesticides Used in the Production of Medical Marijuana in the State of Hawaii, January 2017. It says no products are registered for use on marijuana with EPA or the department and lists requirements for a product that may be used. The page is cut short so that no email address appears.

Part of page 1 of EPA's May 19, 2015 letter to the Colorado Department of Agriculture. It lists five similar-use criteria, including use on food and use on tobacco in order to have a pyrolysis study of breakdown products formed when treated plant material is burned.
slides.credit: Source: EPA letter, May 19, 2015, p. 1, PD

slides.alt: Page 850-111 of the dispensary rules, the start of Table 4 in section 11-850-135. It lists pesticides alphabetically from abamectin with their Chemical Abstracts Service registry numbers.

Part of section 11-850-135(h) of the dispensary rules. It says if any limit is exceeded the dispensary shall not dispense the nonconforming batch, and it lists what may be remediated: heavy metals, foreign or extraneous material, microbial contaminants, mycotoxins and water activity.

Part of page 4 of OMCCR's July 2024 newsletter, a sample certificate of analysis. A callout says all pesticides that are tested are listed and points to Hawaii administrative rules 11-850-135. The page is cut short so that no email address appears.

Part of page 1 of OMCCR's December 2024 newsletter, Know Before You Grow Part 4, with the outdoor pest management bullets. One says to avoid spraying flower buds with pesticides, even organic ones, and to wash buds after harvesting if you do spray.

Part of Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329D-8, as printed from the saved web page. Item (3) says the department shall review and take guidance from the testing programs and standards for pesticides under the regulations of the United States Environmental Protection Agency.

Part of the Hawaii Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity Pesticides Branch web page, printed from the saved copy. It lists a notice about chlorpyrifos and a link to guidance on pesticide use on medical marijuana, dated January 2017.

posts.title: When does a find become a feedstock?
posts.summary: Dutch law says every archaeological find from an excavation must be kept. EX SITU, at Dutch Design Week 2026, worked with finds that were deselected. The government inspectorate's own 2025 report shows how that decision gets made, and what is still unsettled.

slides.alt: A cardboard box of large pale bones and stones, deselected archaeological finds from South Holland, photographed in storage. The vertical EX SITU wordmark is printed at the right edge. The page names mammoth bone among the materials and lists this photograph under Shahar Livne's HUBRIS.

Dark, worn leather pieces including part of a shoe, lying in a clear plastic find bag with a paper label inside. They are deselected finds from South Holland that Judith Sanders reworks in TERRA FIRMA at EX SITU. The bag label is the find documentation the slide asks about; it is only partly legible.

Overhead photograph on white of eight dark bowls holding sorted archaeological materials from South Holland. The STRATA page lists eight materials: flint, mammoth bone, ceramics, wood, glass, iron, natural stone and leather; the photograph does not say which bowl holds which. Natasja van der Meer turns such materials into glazes in STRATA, an experiment shown at DDW 2026 before the finished objects planned for 2027.

A cracked cream-colored Roman jug stands on a bare floor with other pots behind it in a storage room of the Provincial Archaeological Depot of South Holland, photographed in 2009. It shows the kind of storage the fact card refers to.

An aisle with yellow floor markings and a pedestrian symbol beside metal racks that hold dark waterlogged wood and standing stones, with numbered shelf labels. It appears to be the archaeological depot storage floor; the DDW page does not caption it.

Stacked dark archaeological oak logs with cut ends, kept in storage. The DDW page lists this photograph under Daan Simons' Footed Remembrance Pot, made from archaeological wood. The logs are stacked rather than boxed.

A hand holds a medieval Pingsdorf pottery sherd with painted stripes over a table at the Provincial Archaeological Depot of South Holland, with labeled find bags beside it. It shows the handling and study step that is separate from borrowing, photographing and transforming a find.

a Roman ceramic strainer from the Provincial Archaeological Depot of South Holland, with find numbers handwritten on its sherds (find number 42674, Spijkenisse). It is not part of EX SITU; it shows what an identifier on a find looks like.

A necklace by Judith Bloedjes, Thread of Time, made with fragments of archaeological clay pipes strung on a wire with metal rings, photographed on white. It shows how a find is given another interpretation as jewelry in EX SITU.

Iridescent shards of archaeological glass, a bottle neck, bowl bases and curved fragments, lying on a gray tray and in a clear plastic find bag, with the vertical EX SITU wordmark at the right edge. DDW lists this photograph under Bernard Heesen’s glass project at EX SITU. It shows the kind of deselected find the program says the project uses.

Three red Roman sigillata pottery shards on brown card, one a curved rim fragment and two flat pieces with a molded ridge, with the vertical EX SITU wordmark at the left edge. DDW lists this photograph under Lotte Douwes’s Future Unearthed. It shows single pieces whose individual status the essay says it cannot establish.

Close-up of a necklace by Judith Bloedjes: pieces of archaeological flint set in white metal rings joined by a thin wire, photographed alone on white and cropped to the rings. It is the single new object of the close, shown without its source documentation.

onScreen: When does a find become a feedstock?
EX SITU brings deselected South Holland archaeological finds into work by nine designer-artists.
DDW 2026 is described as a first viewing of experiments. Finished objects are planned for 2027.
That stage matters: an experiment on view should not be presented as a completed final work.
Deselected at which stage, by whom, and under which terms?
Seeing, borrowing, photographing and transforming an object are different actions.
The find’s identifier connects its earlier documentation to the new work. A before-and-after picture alone cannot make that link. A Roman ceramic strainer from the Provincial Archaeological Depot.
The artist gives the fragment another interpretation. Which institutional decision made that use possible?

The new object invites attention. What documentation lets us follow its change of use?

posts.title: The Internet Used To Be A Home
posts.summary: Trisha Koevoets framed leaving Big Tech as a house move. EU law gives you two ways to take your data with you. The European Commission's own papers suggest the harder part is finding the door.

slides.alt: A screenshot of the project website: huge white letters Big Tech Verhuis Service over a blue sky, a red starburst reading Claim back your web, and pop-up windows titled Claim back the web and Alert, Verhuis je data, with a blue button reading Niet mijn data (Not my data). Slide text: What would you pack if you moved out of a platform? Trisha Koevoets's project posed as a Big Tech moving service, at Dutch Design Week 2026.

Bar chart titled Which internet do you prefer? The internet of the past got 20 dots, the middle line 3 and the internet of now 3, from dots on the maker's posters in public space in 2026. Slide text: On her street posters, 20 dots went to the old internet. 3 went to today's. A small, self-selected sample. She warned that nostalgia may explain much of it.

The opening words of GDPR Article 20(1), set in type on a pale card, with provided to a controller and without hindrance highlighted, and the Official Journal reference below. Slide text: Since 2018, EU law has let you take the data you gave a service. GDPR Article 20: in a machine-readable format, sent on without hindrance.

A crop of page 10 of the data portability guidelines: a printed paragraph saying the term provided by the data subject should exclude inferred data and derived data, for example algorithmic results. Slide text: What a platform works out about you stays behind. EU guidance leaves inferred and derived data, such as algorithmic results, out of that right.

Digital Markets Act Article 6(9), set in type on a pale card with marked omissions, with free of charge, tools and continuous and real-time access highlighted. Slide text: The EU's Digital Markets Act asks the biggest platforms for more. Free tools, and continuous and real-time access to your data. Article 6(9).

Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: Thousands of users and about 40 third parties use the tools, the Commission says. What we don't: What share of users that is, or how easy the tools are.

posts.title: Haven't Done This Before: Three Days at the Hawaiʻi Cannabis Expo
posts.summary: I hadn't done this before. Hadn't been to the expo. Hadn't been in this community in Hawaii. Downtown Honolulu seen from Puowaina with the Pacific.

onScreen: Haven't Done This Before Three Days at the Hawaiʻi Cannabis Expo
I hadn't done this before. Hadn't been to the expo. Hadn't been in this community in Hawaii. Downtown Honolulu seen from Puowaina with the Pacific.
There were a lot of firsts stacked on top of each other, and the weight of them hit before I'd cleared the entrance.
So I did the only thing I could think of. I found the next task. What is the next step? Just go get your press pass. An empty registration table at a hackathon.
Something clicked back into place: I am a reporter. I asked if I could tape our conversation, and I was surprised by how instantly I felt comfortable in the role. A Zoom H4n handheld audio recorder.
The community had assembled. For three days, it had a home. The Blaisdell Arena beside the Exhibition Hall in Honolulu.
I walked into the Blaisdell Exhibition Hall ready to call my ride. A silver minivan taxi parked on a paved court.
I walked out three days later with twenty-six interviews, a phone full of new contacts, and plans to cover the next expo from inside the community instead of standing at its edge.
The cannabis at the Hawaiʻi Cannabis Expo wasn't what put me on cloud 9. The people did. A flowering Cannabis sativa plant growing outdoors.

posts.title: What does “buy” mean?
posts.summary: A movie bought for $19.99 shows up in a folder called "Purchased." The terms behind the button describe a license that can end. Courts, Congress's advisers and California have each looked at that gap, and the same three questions sit inside every creative deal.

slides.alt: A phone held at an angle showing the iTunes Music Store page for an album: a blue price button sits beside every track (the visible tracks read $15.00) and one beside the album. It opens the story because the price button is the one-tap Buy the sentence describes; the photo shows the buttons, not the terms behind them.

A television wall-mounted in a room showing the Apple TV sign-in screen, with fields for an Apple ID and password and the line asking whether to use different Apple IDs for iTunes and iCloud. It sits under the slide because buying on Apple's services runs through one Apple account, and access follows the service terms tied to it; the photo shows the sign-in, not the terms.

An Amazon Fire tablet on a stand showing its Kindle library of book covers, several with a checkmark for a downloaded copy. It stands for access, the first of the three layers; the photo does not show the usage licence or any copyright.

A first-generation Apple iPad showing the Apple Books (then iBooks) app open to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. It stands for what an Apple purchase delivers, a book you can read inside Apple's app; the photo does not show the Buy button or the terms behind it.

An iTunes gift card printed with the Apple logo, lying on a wooden table. It is a physical way to pay into Apple's store; it is not the store's terms and shows nothing about what a purchase gives you, how you may use it or who owns it.

A worn, blank invoice pad from a Singapore catering supplier, with printed columns for items, quantity and total, lying on gravel beside a small archive tag. It stands for a payment document that lists goods and a total; it is not a creative-work invoice and says nothing about rights.
slides.credit: Photo: My Community SG, CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: A flat lay of eleven removable storage formats on a pale surface: 8-inch, 5.25-inch and 3.5-inch floppy disks, a cassette and an 8mm tape, two CDs, CompactFlash and SD cards, and a USB drive. Each is a different container for delivering files, which is why naming the deliverable matters; the photo does not show a final, editable or source file.

A black-and-white press photograph from January 1936 of men seated around a long council-room table, one signing a document, with rolled plans on the table. It stands for a contract being signed, the moment when questions about change, advertising, transfer and sublicensing belong on paper; it is not about any rights deal in this story.
slides.credit: Photo: Finnish Heritage Agency, CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: A 1954 black-and-white photograph of a hand writing with a pen in a notebook on a table, from a Norwegian national archive. It stands for writing the terms down; it is not the written terms themselves.
A green running-figure exit sign mounted above a wooden door in Australia. It stands for an exit route; it is not a deal document and says nothing about any term or contract.

Photo of a hand holding an Amazon Kindle 2 whose screen reads 'Thank you for your purchase' for a travel guide, with a 'Purchased by Accident? Cancel this Order' link. It shows the moment right after Buy, where the transaction starts; it is Amazon's flow, not Apple's, and does not show the licence language.

posts.title: Your material has a biography. Where is it?
posts.summary: Biomaterials Library brought a Baltic selection to Eindhoven. The public pages for five works, read side by side, show what a material biography keeps and what it still leaves out.

slides.alt: Close-up of PineSkins, a leather-like material made from the inner bark of pine trees, with a ridged, dark red-brown surface in focus. It is one material in the Biomaterials Library collection, shown as the kind of object whose history the slide asks about.

Close view of COFFIRE pendant lamps, ceramic shades with a pink, marble-like surface. The Biomaterials Library page says the pattern comes from coffee grounds releasing biodiesel and sugar during low-temperature firing. It shows coffee grounds after processing; the page does not say which batch they came from.

A large pile of cut pine logs on a cleared yard under a blue sky, from the PineSkins page. The Library page says its leather-like material is made from the inner bark of pine trees, a by-product of the tree-cutting industry. The photograph shows the industry the input comes from, not a documented batch.

Two raised hands in stitched, translucent gloves, one with five fingers and one a mitten, partly lined with an amber, flecked material, against a white ground. It is "Vegetative Textiles" by Indrė Spitrytė-Mikuckė, one of the five works the DDW program page credits for the exhibition. It shows hands in an exhibited object; it documents no handling history for it.

Pieces of PineSkins bark leather laid edge to edge, two hands resting on them, showing the layered texture and cut edges. The Library page says the bark is a by-product of tree cutting and is treated to become flexible; the exact steps are not shown here.

A NewspaperWood sample, newspaper layers cut to show a wood-like grain, lying under a folded newspaper. A printed label card with a QR code and typed fields sits on the sheet. It shows the kind of identifier label the slide asks about; the label text is too small to read.

Rows of material samples on white cards along ledges on a gallery wall, each card with a small caption block, in a white room shown on the Biomaterials Library News and Events page. A visitor and a dog in the original are cropped out.

Close view of dark, rough tiles of Coffee Waste Bio-Resin cladding a counter in an exhibition hall. The Biomaterials Library page says Waste Matters makes the material in Vilnius from coffee residues collected at local cafes.

Many small samples of paper and textile pieces dyed in yellows and oranges, laid out side by side on a white surface, from the Materials page of the Biomaterials Library. It shows how many samples can sit together; the page gives no identifier for each one here.

A white gallery wall of the Biomaterials Library with rows of material samples mounted on white cards along ledges: gold and dark pressed fiber tiles, a rust-colored ring, a dark bark-like panel and cream blocks, each card carrying a small printed label with a QR code. It is the Library's own display from its About page, the kind of documentation that ties each sample to its origin and process; the labels are too small to read here.

A dark, bark-textured vase of the GIRIA collection by Evelina Kudabaitė, holding dried stems against a dark ground, from the Biomaterials Library page. It is one finished listed work. The page outlines the steps (collecting, drying, grinding, boiling a binder, molding) but gives no quantities, which is the kind of recipe this essay does not establish.

A small dark bowl of Coffee Waste Bio-Resin on a white surface. The Biomaterials Library page says Waste Matters makes this thermoplastic in Vilnius from coffee residues gathered at local cafes. It is a finished object made from coffee waste.

A stack of finished GIRIA bowls beside a long strip of rough tree bark, the raw input, on a white surface, from the Biomaterials Library page. It shows the ingredient and the object made from it in one view, the stretch of history the three questions ask about. The photograph does not show who handled the bark or what happened in between.

onScreen: Your material has a biography. Where is it?
Coffee grounds are an ingredient category. Which batch, and what happened to it?
Where did this particular input come from?
Who handled this object, and which handoffs are documented?
Which transformations are documented, and which ingredients remain unstated?
Which document connects the photographed object to that process?
A biography, in this case, is an account of movement.
What is still unknown?

posts.title: Matching Patients and Growers
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi lets a registered caregiver grow medical cannabis for a patient who cannot grow their own. The state publishes how many caregivers there are and no list of who they are. Here is the law behind both facts, and what the numbers show.

The first page of Act 46, Session Laws of Hawaii 2025, S.B. No. 1429, where the first section says some patients may not be able to grow because of limitations such as disability or lack of space.
The definitions section of the medical use of cannabis law, Hawaii Revised Statutes 329-121, including the definition of primary caregiver.

The first page of the Department of Health's August 2026 registry data report, with the in-state patient data box showing patients with a valid registration, applications issued, caregiver totals and physician and APRN totals.

The next page of section 11-160-56, with the remaining exceptions for dispensary system licensees and others deemed necessary by the Department, and the line that the Department may publish non-identifying aggregated data or statistics.

Hawaii Revised Statutes section 92F-14, significant privacy interest, examples, with item (1) on information about medical, psychiatric or psychological history, diagnosis, condition, treatment or evaluation.

A page of OMCCR's September 2026 guide to the in-state patient application, on grow site information, where the patient chooses patient or caregiver for who controls the grow site and who will be growing.

OMCCR's guidance page on Executive Order No. 24-06, which says the order was signed on December 30, 2024 and orders the office to de-prioritize investigation of minor violations by primary caregivers.
The Office of Information Practices page of basic questions and answers on access to government records, with the list of records the law does not require the government to disclose.

posts.title: Who gets credit for a new material?
posts.summary: A close read of the credits for two Dutch Design Week 2026 shows, the 1858 first edition of Gray's Anatomy, and the standards that say what a credit line can and cannot carry.

slides.alt: A folded hemp and wool panel standing in a bright interior beside a window. It is part of "Modulus/Threadline" by Simon Leffler and Martin Vorac, photographed by Maria Michopulu for the UMPRUM project page, with the photographer credited separately. It stands for the exhibition the cover question is about; it is not the entrance or title wall, which does not exist until October 17.

a model in pale clothing holds a woven hemp bag among dark basalt columns. It is "The Hemp Bag" by Anna Sipova, photographed by Emma Lea Nikodymova, the lead image of the SOW HEMP program page. It is not the credit panel, which has not been installed yet; it shows an object and a photograph with different authors.

A large pale relief panel of felted hemp fiber showing figures in motion, standing outdoors on a grass bank. It is "Hyakinthos" by Ferdinand Placak, photographed by Emma Lea Nikodymova, one hemp object from the SOW HEMP exhibition shown as the work itself.

A wooden tray from the Textielmuseum sample cabinet in Tilburg holding hemp stem, fiber, yarn, cord and woven textile. It is the exact file the article cites: the cabinet interior is by Simone de Waart of Material Sense, and the photograph is by Joep Vogels, two different credits for one image.

Illustrative photo: a second tray from the same Textielmuseum cabinet, holding Manila hemp, banana leaf fiber, sisal rope, abaca and raffia in labeled compartments. It shows the cabinet interior (Simone de Waart, Material Sense) next to the photograph (Joep Vogels), the two lines the fact card separates.

a cabinet tray with many different bast fiber samples side by side: raw and spun nettle fiber, hand-tied cords, a glass and nettle-yarn jewelry piece, and woven red and gray cloth. One credit line covers the whole cabinet, while individual pieces such as the jewelry have their own makers.

A leaf-shaped place mat of Manila hemp mesh with a paper maker label sewn to its stalk, photographed flat on white for the Textielmuseum cabinet. The label names the product, while the photographer credit belongs to Joep Vogels; the two are separate pieces of attribution.

A white gallery room of the Biomaterials Library with labeled samples mounted on the walls, two visitors seen from behind, and hanging strips of dark, golden material in the foreground. It shows the curated arrangement the slide asks about: whose contribution is named beside each sample, and whose is missing. The visitors are not identifiable.

A tufted armchair covered in red, orange, black and gray wool and hemp patterns, photographed in warm light. It is "Joy" by Tereza Hlavackova, and the SOW HEMP program page credits it as "c) Tereza Hlavackova, photo Maria Michopulu": the maker and the photographer are named on separate lines.

the inside of a Textielmuseum cabinet tray with its plywood compartments, holding flax stem, fiber, linen cloth and a woven sample. The plywood tray design is by Simone de Waart of Material Sense. A frontal photograph of the whole cabinet does not exist on Commons; this tray shows the cabinet interior design.

Illustrative photo: a plywood tray from the Textielmuseum cabinet in Tilburg holding paper textiles, printed and woven samples, cord and raffia, with a handwritten paper label naming a firm. It is not a colophon or a contract; it shows a sample in the same cabinet whose credits the frame discusses, with a name written beside it.

two people in black balaclavas and yellow safety vests hold up a wooden weaving frame with an orange and gray hemp tapestry. It is "You Are My Star" by Natalie Mala, photographed by Jan Cestr for the SOW HEMP program page. It is not an installation view of the exhibition; the people are anonymous.

onScreen: Who gets credit for a new material?
Designed. Wove. Photographed. Curated. Each verb names a different contribution. A model in pale clothing holds a woven hemp.
The object and its photograph can have different authors.
Those two lines describe different contributions.
Collection-wide or exhibition-wide credits do not explain every individual sample. A cabinet tray with many different bast fiber samples.
An object’s maker marks do not establish the photograph’s reuse rights.
Whose contribution is named, and whose remains missing?
The maker explains who created the object. The photographer explains who created this view of it.
What We Actually Know
The credits are part of the story. Two people in black balaclavas and yellow safety vests.

posts.title: No Standard of Care, No Medical Status, Full Liability: The Facilitator Malpractice Question Oregon's Framework Raises
posts.summary: Oregon's Measure 109 created a new professional category and, in the same set of rules, appears to have disclaimed its clinical character. The entrance of the Portland State Office Building.

The reading room of the Oregon State Archives in Salem, with wooden tables in front of tall windows. The Archives Division of the Secretary of State publishes the Oregon Administrative Rules, which hold the facilitator duty rule.

posts.title: An audience can become a company
posts.summary: Fifty Instagram posts sold out a dress in 2015, and a federal case followed. The documents from that case, and from the rules written since, show the business that sits behind one paid post.

slides.alt: Two pieces of one Federal Register column, September 13, 2017, from the FTC's CSGO Lotto case: according to the complaint, YouTube creators Trevor Martin and Tom Cassell were president and vice president, and both owned the company behind the gambling site their videos promoted.

posts.title: No Organic Seal for Cannabis
posts.summary: One sentence in Hawaiʻi's dispensary rules hands the word organic to Washington, D.C. Here is what federal law does with it, why hemp gets a path that medical cannabis does not, and what the 2026 rescheduling order leaves in place.

slides.alt: Part of a page of the dispensary rules, Hawaii Administrative Rules section 11-850-143. Subsection (g) says a dispensary licensee shall not label as organic any cannabis or manufactured cannabis product unless permitted by the United States Department of Agriculture in accordance with the Organic Foods Production Act.

Part of 7 CFR section 205.2 in the 2025 Code of Federal Regulations. The definition says organic is a labeling term that refers to an agricultural product produced in accordance with the Act and the regulations in this part.

The start of 7 CFR section 205.100, What has to be certified. It says each operation that produces or handles agricultural products intended to be sold, labeled or represented as organic must be certified, except for exempt operations.

Part of 7 U.S.C. section 6502 in the 2024 United States Code. Paragraph (1) defines agricultural product as any agricultural commodity or product, raw or processed, marketed in the United States for human or livestock consumption.

Part of USDA's National Organic Program instruction NOP 2040, effective November 26, 2019. The policy section says only hemp produced under the U.S. Domestic Hemp Production Program or the 2014 Farm Bill may be certified as organic, if produced under the organic regulations.

Part of the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service hemp FAQ, printed from the saved web page. The answer says the legal difference between hemp and marijuana is the amount of THC, and that a hemp license cannot be used to produce medical or recreational marijuana.
slides.credit: Source: USDA AMS, hemp FAQ, Public domain

slides.alt: Part of 21 U.S.C. section 812 in the 2024 United States Code. Schedule I includes item 10, marihuana, and item 17, tetrahydrocannabinols, except for tetrahydrocannabinols in hemp.

Part of page 22719 of the Federal Register of April 28, 2026, in the Drug Enforcement Administration final rule. It says any form of marijuana other than an FDA-approved drug product or marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license remains a schedule I controlled substance.

Part of slide 52 of the Know Before You Grow deck hosted by the Hawaii Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation, cropped to the USDA organic seal and its caption: Federal Cert, but cannabis is still federally illegal, no cert. Part of a photo of a cup of compost tea is also visible.
slides.credit: Source: Hawaiʻi DOH, OMCCR deck, slide 52

slides.alt: Part of the California Department of Food and Agriculture OCal Cannabis Certification Program page, printed from the saved copy. It says only the National Organic Program can authorize the word organic and that cannabis products are not eligible for the organic designation.

Part of page 2 of OMCCR's October 2024 newsletter, in the Nutrients paragraph. It says to use organic nutrients and pesticides, whenever possible, to minimize toxic chemicals in your medical cannabis.

Part of the Federal Register notice of April 28, 2026, page 22777, in which the Drug Enforcement Administration sets a hearing on the proposed rescheduling of marijuana to begin June 29, 2026 and to conclude not later than July 15, 2026.

Part of the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service hemp FAQ, printed from the saved web page. It answers whether hemp produced under the domestic hemp program may qualify for organic certification: it may, under USDA organic regulations.
slides.credit: Source: USDA AMS, hemp FAQ (organic), PD

slides.alt: Part of 7 U.S.C. section 6503, National organic production program, in the 2024 United States Code. Subsection (a) says the Secretary shall establish an organic certification program for producers and handlers of agricultural products produced using organic methods.

posts.title: NAITURE
posts.summary: Merel Mierop's NAITURE set image predictions of decay beside buried fabric. What would make that comparison fair, and what does EU law say about labeling the AI side?

slides.alt: Two dug-up fabric pieces on white: a loose cotton mesh clogged with soil on the left and gray felt with soil and pale roots grown through it on the right. Slide text: An AI guessed how buried fabric letters would decay. Then the letters were dug up. Merel Mierop's NAITURE, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026.

Two lines of printed text from the NAITURE press kit saying that after one month to one year, the letters are dug up and compared with the AI's predictions. Slide text: The letters spent one month to a year underground. An AI got a photo of each letter and a prompt about material, place and conditions, and its guess was set beside the real thing.

Bar chart of weight lost after four months buried in soil: cotton about 90 percent, Tencel 60 percent, PET polyester none, acrylic none. Slide text: The fabric changes what the soil does. In a 2019 burial test, cotton lost about 90 percent of its weight in four months. Polyester lost none.

Bar chart of days for half of each fabric to break down in warm, moist soil: rayon 22, cotton 40, Tencel 94. Slide text: Even plant fabrics rot at different speeds. Buried in warm, moist soil, rayon lost half its mass in 22 days, cotton in 40 and Tencel in 94.

Bar chart of physics scores out of 3 on chemistry scenes for four image models: the best scored 0.84 and the lowest 0.23. Slide text: Image models were weak at picturing chemical change. In a 2024 test with prompts like a rod rusting for decades, the best model scored 0.84 out of 3.

A crop of the Official Journal page that adds paragraph 4 to Article 111: providers of AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026. Slide text: EU law: image generators must mark their output as AI-made. Tools on the market before August 2, 2026 had until December 2, 2026 to comply.

The three EU label icons on a paper band: a black circle with the letters AI, and two black pills that add a word for fully AI-made and partly AI-modified content. Slide text: What We Actually Know. What we know: Letters spent months in soil and were set beside AI guesses. What we don't: The AI model, the number of letters, the soil, the labels.

posts.title: c14-04 Two versions of the law (Tech From Here, second run)
posts.summary: Hawaiʻi has two official languages, and its courts run in one of them. In January 2018 a Maui courtroom found out what happens when a person who speaks both chooses the other. The laws, cases and bills behind that morning reach back to 1896.

slides.alt: A black-and-white photograph from about 1870 of Aliʻiōlani Hale in Honolulu, a two-story stone government building with a clock tower and a tall flagpole in an open yard. It was the Kingdom government building that later housed its Legislature and Supreme Court.
slides.credit: Photo: HABS / Hawaii State Archives, PD
slides.url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_EXTERIOR_VIEW_OF_NORTHEAST_(FRONT)_ELEVATION_FROM_EAST_(Photo_ca_1870,_from_original_in_Hawaii_State_Arvhices).__Photocopy_1966_-_Aliiolani_Hale,_463_King_Street,_Honolulu,_HABS_HI,2-HONLU,3-21.tif (HABS HI-2-HONLU-3-21, 1966 photocopy of a c. 1870 print in the Hawaii State Archives; cropped to the print)

slides.alt: Page 6 of the Compiler's Preface to the 1846 Statute Laws, in old printed type. It says the code went to the king's cabinet for discussion, then to the Rev. William Richards for faithful translation into the native language, then to both houses for three readings, debated section by section.

Page 259 of volume 1 of the Hawaiian Reports, headed 1856, Hardy vs. Ruggles, in old printed type. The lines read that where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian, the latter must govern, because it is the language of the legislators of the country.

Page 367 of the 1859 Civil Code, Chapter XLI, General Provisions, in old printed type. Section 1493 says that if a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian versions of any part of the Code, the English version shall be held binding. The page ends with the approval of May 17, 1859, signed Kamehameha.

Four lines of old printed type from the same page of Hardy v. Ruggles. They read that the English and Hawaiian may often be used to help and explain each other where the meaning is obscure, or the contradiction slight, but where the omission in the Hawaiian is clear, it is impossible to reconcile them.

A printed act headed An Act for the Construction of Statutes Where the English and Hawaiian Versions Do Not Agree. Its one section says that whenever a radical and irreconcilable difference is found between the English and Hawaiian version of any of the laws of the Kingdom, which have been, or may hereafter be enacted, the English version shall be held binding. Approved January 10, 1865, signed Kamehameha R.
slides.credit: Source: Laws of 1864 to 1865, p. 68, PD

slides.alt: A 1943 session-law page headed Promulgation of Laws. Act 218 rewrites the rule so that the secretary of the Territory publishes the laws once in the English language in a Honolulu daily newspaper. The Hawaiian-language publication is gone from the text.

Two crops of a 1979 session-law page, Act 97, S.B. No. 45. It rewrites section 1-13: English and Hawaiian are the official languages of Hawaii; where there is a radical and irreconcilable difference between the English and Hawaiian version of any state law, the English version shall be held binding; Hawaiian shall not be required for public acts and transactions.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 16, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined new text adds a proviso to section 1-13: if a law was originally drafted in Hawaiian and its English version was translated from it, and the law has not been subsequently amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English, the Hawaiian version shall be held binding.

A typed bill page, S.B. No. 109, S.D. 2, H.D. 1, with numbered lines. Underlined text adds the same proviso for laws originally drafted in Hawaiian and not later amended, codified, recodified or reenacted in English. Its last line reads: This Act shall take effect on July 1, 3000.

A typed bill page, H.B. No. 2433, H.D. 1, S.D. 1, with numbered lines. The sentence making the English version binding is struck through. New underlined text gives priority to the language that aligns with the intent of the legislature as evidenced by legislative history, context and purpose. The last line sets the effective date at March 22, 2075.

Seven lines of old printed type from page 480 of volume 8 of the Hawaiian Reports, April 1892, In re Ross. They read that the English version shall be held binding, that the two versions constitute but one act, that there is no dual legislation, and that as a rule one version is the translation of the other.

The top of page 69 of volume 2 of the Hawaiian Reports, 1858, Levi Haalelea v. Daniel Montgomery, in old printed type. It reads that the deed is a printed formula in two languages, that the English version of this formula is, of course, the original, and the Hawaiian merely a translation.
